the next item is the report by mr giusto catania, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the fourth report on citizenship of the union (1 may 2001 - 30 april 2004) (2005/2060 (ini)) (a6-0411/2005).
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the recognition of citizenship and the rights attaching to it is a prerogative of the member states. the european citizenship is a concept in the making, a right derived from national citizenship. the fact that each country has different procedures for recognising national citizenship means that there is no uniform procedure for obtaining european citizenship. the report, for which i am rapporteur, does not call into question the prerogative of the member states: the right to citizenship and its recognition are their prerogatives, as expressly recognised by the treaties. perhaps the time is not ripe yet, and i have seen this reflected in the debate in the committee on the harmonization of the procedures for the recognition of citizenship. however, i think it is extremely useful and necessary to start thinking - in a short time - about the real and effective value of the concept of european citizenship. in my view - and this is not just my view but also the view of the majority of the committee on civil liberties - the only way to give real value to the concept of european citizenship is to link it intimately to that of residence. the european citizenship of residence is a very serious issue and this debate has involved thousands of associations and intellectuals who have already started a petition for the activation of this institute. european citizenship of residence can also be combined with the other forms of recognition of citizenship, namely citizenship by right of blood or ius solis, which are provided for in many countries of the european union. i believe that the recognition of residence citizenship is a way of eliminating and avoiding certain paradoxes: i think it is unfair to consider as a european citizen someone who works, lives and resides legally in the territory of the union, a citizen who has lived and worked in a member state for ten or twenty years, but who unfortunately was born to tunisian or egyptian parents. i believe that blood, place of birth and residence can, together and at the same time, constitute valid elements for the recognition of the right to citizenship. the fact that after five years of legal residence in europe one can become a citizen of the union seems to us a practical way of reopening the debate on the future of europe, which, after the rejection of the constitutional treaty, has plunged into a crisis that risks being lethal and irreversible. some rights attached to citizenship of the union are already conferred on the basis of residence: i am referring to the right to petition the european parliament or to the right to address the ombudsman. the right to move and reside freely and the right to vote in european and local elections can therefore be extended to include citizens of the union residing in a country other than their own. this would be an important step towards the integration of the many non-eu citizens who are living in europe on a regular basis. i would also ask my colleagues in the group of the european people's party to support this position and to abandon their overly extreme positions. the proposed document, in addition to having the support of my group, the socialist group, the greens and the liberal group in the committee, also had the support of the commission, whose officials expressed a positive opinion in the committee on civil liberties on the activation of residence citizenship. commissioner frattini also expressed his readiness to provide support in this direction. i think this is a very important step, which has also been endorsed by many social, trade union and civil society organisations, both secular and catholic: i am referring to two major italian organizations, such as caritas, and a major catholic trade union, such as cisl, which have publicly expressed their support for this report, in order to establish residence citizenship. finally, i would like to reassure those who, in their comments on this report, have raised the spectre of the introduction of a european tax to extend citizenship rights. among them is even the italian prime minister, who in a recent television broadcast incorrectly stated that this parliament wants to introduce a tax to extend citizenship. for the avoidance of doubt, although i do not see the danger in this report, i propose that we eliminate the explicit reference to the european tax and concentrate exclusively on the concept of citizenship of residence. i hope that this will also help to remove some of the alibis of those who are afraid of extending rights in europe.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on tuesday at 12 noon.

is not just the issue of women, it is the issue of the whole society, it is the issue of all actors in society. the commission intends to work on this problem in this context. i would also like to say that i share the main points that have been expressed in this house and that i have listened to with great attention. i do not agree with certain interventions that encourage the retention of stereotyped roles for women, even of a different age. it is not women's work that causes unemployment. this is an argument that is heard too often in certain circles and it is obviously against this type of argument that we must fight, because it prevents significant progress in some countries. what is the commission doing about this? i would like to remind you that the demands that have been made are essentially national policies. it is still up to the states to legislate on the major issues raised. i am of course aware that the commission has a role to play and i will explain in what areas it intends to intervene and how. the new integrated guidelines clearly reaffirm the need to mainstream gender in all employment policies and reaffirm the need to promote gender equality in all actions undertaken. the new employment strategy includes the target of 60% employment by 2010. it includes in the guidelines, inter alia, the elimination of gender gaps and the promotion of work-life balance. the commission has also made mainstreaming a fundamental principle of community action. i would remind you that it is enshrined as such in article 3 of the treaty establishing the european community. mainstreaming is implemented through a community framework strategy on equality between women and men. the strategy aims to establish a framework for action in which all community activities, including economic activities and policies as well as employment policy, can contribute to the objective of eliminating inequalities and promoting equality between women and men. the commission is currently preparing a roadmap for equality between men and women, which will take over from the framework strategy from 2007. like the commission, it will aim at the effective implementation of gender mainstreaming in all community policies, and in particular the lisbon strategy. i would like to say a word about the pay gap. the gender pay gap is a complex phenomenon, which is not just a result of discrimination. this is the result of several factors, such as the segregation of the labour market, the persistence of stereotypes, especially in education and training, and the difficulty of reconciling work and private life. the question is therefore to address all the underlying factors. it is worth emphasizing the particular attention we intend to give to reducing the pay gap in the employment strategy. two guidelines explicitly call for action by the member states and the social partners. it should also be noted that the austrian presidency has announced that it will be holding a conference on the pay gap at the end of may in brussels, and i think that this will be a rather exceptional opportunity to make further progress in this area. a word on how to study and analyse the changing position of women in the labour market from the point of view of knowledge of their rights and the role of men. the commission shall monitor equality policy on an ongoing basis and shall regularly carry out or arrange for the carrying out of analyses and studies on economic and legal aspects of equality. the annual report on equality between men and women, presented by the commission since 2004 at the spring summit of heads of state and government, is a very important document for monitoring the issue of gender equality in the european union. the report sets out the main developments in the respective situations of women and men in education, employment and social life. it identifies progress made and challenges still to be addressed. the commission is also analysing the member states' national reform programmes in the context of lisbon in this light, which will be an important contribution to the employment chapter of the annual monitoring report. how does the commission intend to improve the statistical methodology to take account of the gender dimension? the integration of the gender dimension is of course implemented in the statistical field. this requires a statistical methodology and the use of gender-sensitive statistics. as the draft resolution stresses, the availability of adequate, consistent and comparable statistical indicators is absolutely essential for monitoring policies. eurostat is actively collaborating with the national statistical institutes to develop a common methodology for collecting reliable and comparable data at european level. it is important that this data is collected at this level. the future gender institute should also make a significant contribution to improving the statistical monitoring of equality policy. i would like to remind you, however, because i think it is useful to state the facts, that this institute will be primarily a technical instrument and will in no way be a political body or a provider of financial resources. this is the commission's reply, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, which fully shares the concerns expressed in the report and once again congratulates the rapporteur on his excellent work.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, honourable members, thank you for your valuable views on the white paper. first of all, action must follow. if we talk about reaching out to citizens we cannot cut down on the programmes where we actually do just that. on this point, we have exactly the same position as the european parliament as far as i understand. we want a budget which hopefully is increased and definitely not reduced. this is also our position in the ongoing budget negotiations. we will make our views absolutely clear on that. we certainly hold the same position on that issue. mr wiersma, i think you made a very valid point, because this is also about the participation of citizens. i have repeated that democracy is not just a spectator sport. it requires an engagement from citizens, but they also have to be able to acquire the basic knowledge about what is going on and how to exert influence. there is therefore also an obligation on us to make sure that there is access, for example, to civic education, where one can learn how it all works and how one can have a voice in this process. i think the services directive is a very good example of how simply telling the story does not help if the basis is not there, if the consultation has not been carried out. in the end we will have nobody advocating the proposal. i think that this is an example of where we really have to do the repair work. this is about engaging citizens. yesterday, one of my colleagues at a commission meeting said that when the commission consulted children about a proposal on children’s rights, the proposal which came back had been completely turned around. children have another order of priorities. we learned a lot from that consultation process. this is what it is all about. it is about the ethics of communication. it cannot be disconnected from the policy because communication can only be as good as its content. it has to be about the policy content, what we want to do to change the reality of things. however, we also have to clarify which rules and attitudes towards democracy and democratic procedure we adopt. we must also clarify how communication and the ethics of communication are an essential tool in helping us. that is what we are establishing here: the tools, framework and procedures that enable us to communicate, to have a two-way dialogue with citizens. that is what we are trying to build here. you are correct to ask about the budget. we are only asking for a few more staff to help during the whole consultation period. it is too early to say what we need for the concrete proposals because we are carrying out consultations about that. we have to come back on the specific proposals and action plans with proper impact assessments, budgets and concrete figures. for the moment, we are only setting the consultation period and putting that in place. when i heard mr bonde’s description, i wondered whether we had been reading the same document. i have to respond to the whole issue of a press agency and this is partly a language issue. we have never had any other idea than to upgrade the service that exists today within the directorate-general for communications. it is called ‘europe by satellite’. we have very few people to carry out the service that provides pictures and sound for radio and television all over europe. we do it in 20 languages. if we want to have better quality and more facts and figures and to better cover what happens in the council, parliament and the commission, then we will need more staff and equipment. as i said earlier, this is how we help regional television or radio stations that cannot afford to send correspondents to brussels. if we are serious about providing that inside, interinstitutional information, then we need the people to do it. in the end, we will need a highly professional person to decide what is most interesting from a journalistic point of view: should we send out a team to parliament today, or should it be in another place covering a different story? we already do that, but with very few resources. this does not conflict with the web-tv that parliament has already decided to invest in, which covers what happens inside the institution, but complements efforts to better communicate with citizens. this has been the idea from the outset. the brussels-based journalists are not happy. they see a risk of competition. i see very little competition in covering press conferences in 20 languages. i do not think this is a problem. however, everybody is trying to cover their territory. we have to be realistic. if we want the stories out there, at local and regional level and on radio and tv – which are the sources that most of our citizens use today to get information about what happens in the eu – then we need to invest in radio and tv. we are the only ones who can provide these pictures and sounds from inside the institutions. nobody will be competing with us on that. this is what we want to do with our proposal in the white paper. there was no vote on this. we have discussions and very rarely vote in the commission. during the whole five years of the prodi commission we held votes only about five or ten times. so there was no vote, but strong support for my white paper. i am glad to be able to tell you that. this is not only about voting. you are right in saying that we must tell the citizens that this is another political arena and that political discussion is crucial. we need to debate. we will have different ideological viewpoints on issues and the discussion will go on in the european arena. we have to help citizens to be able to follow and understand what goes on and to have a say. you will find some ideas on how to do that in our white paper. finally, i agree with mr hammerstein mintz. i hope we will see a pilot project where council meetings will become open. this is also a way to end the blame game, where the institutions blame each other. in the end it is the citizens who lose out, because they are unable to follow or judge what is going on and what their ministers say in the council. i agree that council meetings should be open and citizens should be able to follow them. we will contribute whatever we can to make that possible. it is also the commission’s position that openness and transparency are absolutely crucial in the context of improving communications.

economic, social and cultural rights in the broad sense, must be at the heart of european union policy. the clause was introduced in the early 1990s with the lomé convention and was also applied to argentina in 1990. in its annual report, the european parliament calls each year for this clause to take on greater significance and urges the council to give parliament a greater role in monitoring its application. so far parliament's requests have not been satisfactorily answered. the clause is now included in more than 50 agreements and applied in more than 120 countries. in this connection, the importance of the cotonou agreement, signed with the acp countries in june 2000, which has strengthened the role of this clause, should be emphasised. the first point i would like to make is about the european parliament. the council must give its assent to an agreement before it enters into force, but it is not called upon to give its opinion on the opening of consultations or on the partial suspension of an agreement. this undermines its institutional and, more generally, political role. i therefore think it is important to stress that parliament is no longer prepared to give its opinion on new international agreements which do not contain a clause on human rights and democracy. parliament feels that it should be involved in defining the negotiating mandate for new agreements with third countries and, above all, in drawing up their political objectives and the promotion of human rights. parliament also asks to be involved in the decision-making process on the opening of consultations or the suspension of an agreement, or the suspension of any negative appropriate measures already imposed on a country. parliament also called for its involvement in the association council and the subcommittees on human rights and for its interparliamentary delegations to play a greater role in this respect by regularly including the democratic clause on the agenda of its meetings. another point i would like to make is the reciprocity between the european union and third countries, which has not been fully exploited so far. i also believe that the clause should be applied in relation to the infringement in question and not in relation to the country in question. it is also necessary to extend the clause to all new agreements between the european union and third countries - industrialized or developing - including sectoral agreements and trade, technical or financial aid, following the example of what has been achieved so far for the acp countries. it is necessary to provide for the systematic inclusion of human rights issues on the agenda of the association council. in this connection, it is felt that the head of the commission's external delegations in third countries should play a more important role and calls for the preparation of multiannual country-by-country strategy papers, which should be discussed regularly. it also provides for a structured dialogue between the association council and its subcommittee on human rights. the committee calls for the establishment of general subcommittees on human rights to monitor compliance with, and the application and implementation of, the democratic clause and to propose specific positive actions aimed at improving democracy and human rights. it is important to emphasise that the inclusion and consultation of representatives of parliaments and civil society organisations in these subcommittees is requested. there is another extremely important aspect. in this resolution we acknowledge that the application of the clause has so far been made more difficult by the requirement of unanimity in the council for the initiation of a consultation procedure. the committee therefore calls for the abolition of unanimity and, to this end, for the revision of article 300 (2) of the treaty establishing the european community, which limits the role of the european parliament in these cases. finally, while it is believed that the clause should apply to all countries and all agreements, it is also believed that agreements could be signed with the countries concerned by the new neighbourhood policy which go beyond the democratic clause, based on the sharing of common institutions for the promotion of democratic principles and human rights, following the example of the council of europe and regional agreements.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think we are all absolutely convinced of the need to complete the internal market in services by eliminating barriers, overlapping and protectionist measures. this is a real and widespread problem. however, the initial choices proposed in the bolkestein directive were contradictory and in many ways ambiguous and wrong. the fundamental mistake was that we triggered opposite and negative perceptions. on the one hand, the impression that the revival of virtuous competition was essentially a license for social and democratic dumping. on the other hand, as a result of the more than legitimate resistance to these ambiguities, many countries, especially newcomers, feel that they want to consolidate or defend protectionist barriers and obstacles to the free movement of services. i believe that today, on the basis of the compromise texts presented, it is possible to correct these contradictions and these shortcomings in a substantial way. a well-founded criticism concerns certain exclusions and derogations in certain sectors, which have a real negative impact on the prospects for competitive growth in european production, economic and social systems, such as professional activities, banking, financial and insurance services and energy supplies. many say that the mountain is in danger of giving birth to the mouse. in reply to these objections, i would point out that it is preferable to take this risk than to give birth to a scorpion, since the poison deposited in the tail of this little animal would above all have polluted the balance of the european social model.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr letta, and all the members of the committee on economic and monetary affairs for the excellent work they have done on the proposal for a regulation on this type of statistics. i would like to stress in particular the fact that the work of parliament has recognised the need to have the data required by this regulation available as soon as possible. it is not necessary to recall that our most direct competitors, the united states and japan, have had detailed data on the investments of their companies abroad for more than twenty years and, as a result, their governments and their economic players have a comparative advantage over europe, which is not negligible when designing their policies or their commercial strategies. the commission therefore considers it highly desirable that parliament and the council can reach agreement on this proposal for a regulation at first reading, so that the collection of this type of data can begin this year. i understand that both institutions are very close to an agreement and we want to see it as soon as possible. the regulation, as i have said, responds to a gap in community statistics which puts us at a disadvantage. at present, we only have data that some member states collect on a voluntary basis, either in the framework of structural economic statistics or in compiling their balance of payments data. but these data cannot be aggregated at the eu-25 level, because of the diversity of methodologies or the type of information compiled. it goes without saying that we all attach great importance to the lisbon strategy and its objectives of increasing growth and employment, of making the european union an attractive area for investment and business, and of completing the internal market. we are also in a year in which the importance of defending european interests in multilateral trade negotiations is particularly evident. the data which this regulation aims to obtain are of great use for all this. in short, ladies and gentlemen, we are talking about a type of statistics which is crucial to ensuring greater dynamism, vitality and competitiveness for european businesses and economic actors. in this connection, the commission considers that the amendments tabled and discussed by the honourable members, which are designed to speed up the start of the compilation of these data, provide an excellent basis for reaching a compromise at first reading. for the same reason, the commission does not share the need to maintain amendments concerning the role of parliament in the development of the regulation, because given the eminently technical nature of the regulation, such amendments would bring relatively little added value, but would almost certainly prevent an agreement with the council at first reading; i am referring, of course, to amendments nos 1, 2 and 9, which seek to extend to the field of the compilation of statistical data the procedures of the so-called lamfalussy process, concerning legislation on financial services. the honourable members, and in particular the members of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, which is also responsible for the financial services directives, are in a privileged position to appreciate the differences between the two sectors. it is not necessary to recall here the different levels of development of the legislation on financial services and the reasons, very different from the case which brings us here today, why the commission considered it appropriate that, at some of these levels, parliament should have a greater scrutiny capacity than that granted to it by the existing rules on comitology. however, before i conclude, i would like to draw your attention to two factors in an attempt to persuade you to reconsider your position on these three amendments: 1, 2 and 9. first, account should be taken of the existing agreement between the institutions to set, by the codecision procedure, the final parameters concerning the compilation of data once the results of the pilot studies are known. parliament will thus have full power, together with the council, to exercise its legislative role in the essential aspects of the implementation of this regulation. secondly, i would like to recall the political will of the austrian presidency to reach a satisfactory agreement with parliament on the revision of the rules on comitology. as you know, there is a commitment in this area which will more equitably reflect the legitimate aspirations of parliament to play its full role as legislator. in these circumstances, mr president, and while i would of course reiterate the commission's constant readiness to keep parliament informed of the work of the various committees, i hope that your vote will facilitate an agreement on this regulation at first reading.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the commission and commissioner almunia for their comments and for the valuable work that the two institutions have done during the preparatory phase of this debate. with this directive, which is very important despite its apparent technical nature, we want to regulate two types of data on foreign subsidiaries, namely inward statistics, which cover all enterprises and all sectors under foreign control, and outward statistics, which relate to companies abroad controlled by a company established in the european union. as commissioner almunia said, the commission is proposing to establish a mandatory reference framework for the compilation of community statistics on the structure and activities of foreign subsidiaries. the commission proposal provides for two different models for the collection of inward and outward data. the model for inwards fats is based on the regulation of structural business statistics, while for outwards fats the model used for foreign direct investment in the regulation for balance of payments statistics is referred to. while inwards would be mostly mandatory, the provisions for outwards provide for a voluntary experimental phase through pilot studies to establish the cost-effectiveness of data collection. the critical element of this directive is that, as commissioner almunia has just mentioned, the united states and japan have had this kind of information for over 20 years, at a level of detail even higher than that which the directive seeks to introduce. the commission's proposal provides for pilot studies and comitology procedures with long transition periods. this risks leaving european policymakers without adequate data for too long, while american and japanese counterparts can already have better information on the strategies and economic trends of their own companies and transnational corporations, including on the outward. for all these reasons, we believe that the commission's proposal should be supported, but with certain requirements. first, the provisions of these regulations must not constitute an excessive bureaucratic and financial burden for the undertakings concerned. secondly, the time taken for the regulation to be implemented and, consequently, for the data to be available should not be too long, so that european policy makers can be placed in the same position as their american and japanese counterparts as soon as possible. the comitology procedure, which has been widely discussed in our committee as an alternative to the legislative procedure for the implementation of the outward fats, must be evaluated very carefully and in the awareness that the objective of the short-term availability of homogeneous data will have to be pursued with every effort. finally, the european central bank and other institutions which have a particular interest in the availability of adequate statistical information should be involved in the definition of common standards. our discussion in the run-up to today's debate was an open confrontation between parliament, the commission and the council. we have always tried to reach a compromise which would lead to the adoption of the directive at first reading as soon as possible. however, the impression that there was no will in the council to bring this text to a positive conclusion at first reading leads us to consider the discussions which have taken place in committee on the subject of comitology as a matter which parliament must bear in mind, particularly when voting on the amendments on comitology. for all these reasons, i think it is useful and important to recommend to this house that it should vote in favour of the directive. this is an important vote because it makes our european system on the international trade side more sensitive to competitiveness data. from the outset we have aimed at the adoption at first reading of this directive, which, beyond its apparent technicality, has a very important content which leads me to suggest to this house that it should be voted on as soon as possible.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this report is a major step forward in the understanding of the concept of the 'information society'. i would like to draw particular attention to one aspect of the report, namely that it accurately indicates the very close link between the impressive technological developments under way and the fate of democracy. it was right to show the effects of the information society on growth and employment and to outline the benefits, the problems and also the remedies. but the implications are much broader: the media have already become decisive in shaping the thoughts and behaviors of billions of individuals. their role is therefore socially relevant, often decisive. their ownership cannot be separated from responsibility to society, their effects cannot be seen in market terms alone. all our values, our rights, even the fate of peace and the survival of mankind are at stake in this issue. we are not only faced with a series of economic and technical problems, but also with fundamental rights such as the right of everyone to be informed, to express himself and to communicate, without forgetting that the information society will increasingly be a society of moving images. this will be the dominant language of the future. those who cannot decipher the images and defend themselves against their manipulation will not be free: helping our children learn this language will be the only way to make them conscious citizens.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. the information society must be open to all, it must be an element of democracy which takes account of cultural diversity and which encourages the participation of citizens as protagonists and not as mere consumers. the issue of closing the digital divide, a problem of balanced development, but above all of social justice, must be tackled. the role of public investment in safeguarding the open nature of the fta is essential in order to ensure the development of technical and cultural means enabling all citizens to benefit from an ever-increasing volume of communication and information services. in order to achieve good governance and guarantee all europeans full citizenship, a european charter of the rights of consumers in the digital world, the so-called e-rights, with shared principles and guidelines, which define the framework of citizens' rights, must be adopted. the charter must include in particular the right to free and open access, and therefore non-discriminatory, to transparent, pluralistic and comprehensive information in a secure environment through telecommunications services and platforms based on open and interoperable standards, for example the portability of e-mail addresses. with the i-2010 directive, europe has a key role to play in ensuring that the information society is accessible to all.

member of the commission. mr president, if you do not mind i shall not go along the course of answering the point about bed linen at this precise moment. in the time i have available i think it would be better to stick to shoes, but i can assure you that the question of any anti-dumping duty on bed linen will be properly assessed and properly applied as, in my opinion, it is at the moment. i think that the value of debates such as this and the important role of this parliament are demonstrated by the very important and insightful observations that have been made during the last 45 minutes. my role on behalf of the commission is to listen to what honourable members have to say and to reflect very carefully on the points and arguments that have been raised. i can assure you i will reflect on them and on the observations made by member states so that when i come back to the commission with final recommendations i will be able to do so having heard the variety, diversity and range of different points and arguments that have been made. however, having heard so many people this afternoon complain that my intervention is protectionist, unnecessary and unjustified, alongside a slightly greater number of members of this house who have complained that i am not going far enough, my actions are inadequate and that i should go further, i am tempted to make the easy observation that perhaps i have got the measures just about right between those two rival points of view! however, tempting as it is to make that rather cheap observation, i am going to avoid doing so. i should like to say, though, that i agree particularly with mr papastamkos and mrs saïfi, both of whom see the need to intervene against anti-competitive and trade-distorting behaviour by our partners, but at the same time to do so with a degree of perspective and balance that i think it behoves me to uphold. i think mr assis is right in that, in the provisional measures that are introduced, it is important that we maintain careful monitoring and surveillance of the effect of what we are doing so as to ensure that, if there is circumvention of our duties, we are able to review the situation and perhaps take revised action when we come to the definitive stage of our measures later this year. let me very quickly respond to some of the other points that have been made. some have drawn a parallel between the proposed action on shoes and the action that we took on textiles. they are very different cases. in the case of textiles, we were dealing with fairly-traded goods, albeit subject to a dramatic and sudden increase in volume following the lifting of quotas on chinese textiles at the beginning of 2005. we therefore took a safeguard measure by the introduction of quotas, as we are entitled to do. we were not, as in this case, dealing with anti-competitive measures – dumping actions – that attract an anti-dumping measure in the form of a tariff duty – not a quota and not a physical limit. therefore i do not anticipate our running into the temporary teething problems that we had in the case of textiles. this should be remembered by those who describe the textile period as involving us in some sort of war or battle with china. far from it. we were able to agree with china the measures that we took, in a very unwarlike way. two other points were raised by a number of members. one concerns the impact on consumer prices. let us put this case into perspective. it concerns only nine pairs of shoes from every 100 pairs bought by european consumers; in other words, a fraction of the product range. a duty would be just over eur 1.50 on average wholesale prices of eur 8.50 on shoes which then sell for between eur 40 and eur 120, as opposed to a duty which would simply amount to eur 1.50. please do not tell me that eur 1.50 cannot be absorbed across the supply chain by importers and retailers, especially importers and retailers who have benefited from low import prices from china and vietnam but who have not passed on the effects of those cheaper import prices to consumers – a question that consumers may put to their retailers if they are able to encounter them at some stage in the future. a number of members have asked me why i am proposing to exclude sports technology shoes and children’s shoes. in the case of the sports shoes, these are excluded from the investigation because they are not produced in europe in sufficient quantity to qualify as being potentially harmed by dumping. there is therefore no injury to european producers because they barely exist in the case of these sports shoes. in the case of children’s shoes, the exclusion i am proposing is on the grounds of community interest. young children need three to four pairs of new shoes per year. the impact of a duty on the price of such shoes is therefore potentially greater than it is for ordinary shoes. in my view, parents should not see any potential hurdles put in the way of buying good-quality shoes for their children. those who want me to reclassify the customs segmentation for these shoes should bear in mind that the customs classification for children is up to size 37½ with heels less than 3cm. whilst i am prepared to discuss that with my colleagues in taxud, it is a classification that i am given, not one that i propose. let me make just briefly one or two other quick observations. there was a suggestion that the investigation had taken too long. this sampling takes time. i am obliged by the regulations that exist within the european community to observe very strict procedures and use very strict reference countries and companies when i am investigating those of another country that does not enjoy market economy status. therefore, just as i cannot anticipate dumping complaints – some members were complaining that i do not show enough foresight, as if i have a crystal ball before me that is going to reveal where the next dumping complaint is going to come from – i cannot pre-empt proper procedures and investigations that are laid out in our regulations and which i am obliged to follow in detail. let me reply to the suggestion that somehow there was a breach of confidentiality. i do not understand this. member states received the commission’s working document before my press conference on 23 february. the moment these working documents go out to member states i can assure you that they are as good as published to the media. i therefore have to clarify them immediately and explain and justify what i am doing. this certainly does not deprive member states of their right to express an opinion on the case or to receive detailed replies from the commission’s services. i shall leave the matter there, except to say in conclusion that it is very important that we see what is happening in china, vietnam, india and other asian countries in some perspective. of course there is tough competition and there is a difficult challenge for european producers and manufacturers to rise to, and we have an obligation to do everything we can to help european producers rise to this challenge and to help those employed in companies adjust to the challenges and the new circumstances of international trade which we are experiencing. i do not believe that a proper and legitimate way of helping people to adjust to these new forces in the global economy is to encourage people to shelter from them or to pretend that, if we close our eyes or cover our heads with a blanket, these changes, challenges and new sources of competition will somehow go away and leave us alone so that we do not have to respond to them. any politician giving that sort of message to the public would be guilty of false leadership, and poor leadership to the public, who need to understand what is going on and help to respond to it. we cannot maintain the pretence that we in europe, by retreating from the competitive challenge we are facing in the global economy, will somehow be able to hide from it and, at the same time, maintain our living standards and our prosperity in the future. we cannot and will not do that. we have to respond to this challenge by putting the emphasis on our competitiveness, innovation and ability to respond to change and to compete more effectively in the future. if we do not rise to that challenge and do not set that out to our public, we cannot blame them subsequently for reacting with fear and mystification to what is taking place in the global economy. (applause)
member of the commission. mr president, china is not yet qualified to receive recognition of market economy status by europe. there are technical criteria that china needs to fulfil, and it is making progress towards doing so. indeed we can, should and are giving every assistance to china to enable it more easily and rapidly to make the technical changes that will enable it to fulfil those criteria. it is important to do that. let me add this related comment. the environment in which member states and members of this house come to judge the market economy status of china will be helped and encouraged by china doing more than it is at the moment to open its markets to our exports and to others’ trade, to make sure that it is in full compliance with its wto accession commitments, and to make sure that where it is taking longer than is reasonable to move towards full compliance with those commitments and wto rules it makes the necessary changes sooner rather than later. if china were to do that, and to respond to the anxieties felt in europe and around the world about the growth of its export capacity in a way that rebalanced the terms of trade – so that as well as people seeing goods coming in ever-growing numbers from china, they were also to see those containers being refilled and returned to china with european and other goods – it would do more than anything else to still public anxiety about what we are seeing in china. understandably, people in europe see the growth of china’s market as a threat, but we must understand it as a huge opportunity for us in europe to sell our own goods and services to that market in future. however, china has a responsibility to make sure that no artificial or unreasonable barriers remain in place to european goods and services being sold to the chinese market in ever-growing numbers. when we get that equation right, then perhaps people will be able to look more sympathetically, as well as technically, at the issue of china’s market economy status. the european arrest warrant must be assessed by analysing the overall impact of the framework decision on judicial cooperation, the mutual recognition of criminal offences, and respect for individual guarantees and civil liberties. unfortunately, we are in a very difficult situation today, some member states have shown difficulties in implementing it because they are hampered even by their national constitutions. however, it would be wrong to think that we should impose twists on national constitutions to guarantee the arrest warrant. today's assessment, unfortunately, has to be independent of the data of a country: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are not used to the detriment of the member states. finally, it is not possible to think of establishing the european arrest warrant without first establishing common minimum standards of criminal procedure and without providing for shared guarantees. parliament has already spoken on minimum procedures, and we expect the council to take further action on this point. it was like building a palace from the roof instead of the foundation. the european arrest warrant can certainly be a useful instrument to remove the political will for the extradition of criminals, and there are already some positive examples of this, but the procedure is tainted by an original vice, an original sin, which arose from the haste of having to respond to terrorist attacks with emergency legislation. i very much agree with the assessment made by mr hazan in his report. the text was improved in committee, even avoiding extending the list of 32 offences, but our assessment cannot but derive from the false start caused by the obsession with security. there's an old italian proverb that says: "the cat in a hurry made the kittens blind". this metaphor can be applied perfectly to the assessment of the first year of application of the european arrest warrant.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are indeed facing a very important situation for europe: the member states are still bound to the perception of a national dimension which is regarded as the dominant one, while we forget that there has been a leap in size and that we must consciously move towards a continental dimension, knowing that we are moving in that direction and also knowing how to govern it. that is why i cannot understand the difficulties that have arisen, for example in the case of the mergers of banks in poland, and we in italy have accepted a takeover of the banca nazionale del lavoro in this very perspective. i see a conflict of interest in these difficulties, precisely because very often these are wholly public companies or at least majority public companies. it is a conflict of interest between the immediate political interest and the long-term interest, not only of consumers but also of the overall efficiency of the european system. this is what has happened in the case of enel and suez, where a major conflict of interest emerges between the need to rationalise our companies so that they can really compete on a global scale and the need to avoid their being mortified on such a short-term scale. i ask that competition be organized as well; we also discussed this with commissioner kroes this morning, and i thank her for her willingness to discuss energy competition. the electricity, gas and electricity networks must be set up at a european level. this is our mission and i urge swift action on this matter.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the unification of markets is a fundamental objective of the union, but it is also more than that: the market is one of the pillars on which the whole process of european integration has been built and is based. a real market requires first of all that capital should move freely and be placed where it is best remunerated; secondly, companies are taking on a cross-border dimension and establishing themselves where they consider it most attractive for their competitiveness through mergers and acquisitions, even hostile ones. the market does not tolerate abuses of dominant positions which impede free competition. an open and well-functioning market is crucial for europe's competitiveness on international markets. the protectionism we have seen in recent months has the opposite effect. with states blocking takeovers, cross-border mergers or acquisitions to protect national strategic interests. in reality, protectionism is designed to defend weak and inefficient firms or to artificially create national champions. the damage it causes is significant for users, who cannot get the best prices for goods and services, and is serious for the community, which has to bear the costs of noncompetitive enterprises. it should be added that protectionism by its very nature is not able to guarantee workers a secure and lasting employment prospect. europe is going backwards with protectionism. in order to function properly, the market must be efficient, there must be no asymmetries. everyone has to follow the rules: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we therefore call on the european commission to take firm action to ensure the free movement of capital and free competition. we therefore welcome what has been said to mrs kroes in this house. the courage to make these choices means being a serious europeanist: the european parliament has been a key player in the process of european integration, and it is the european parliament which has been the driving force behind the process of european integration.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are faced with two possible mergers. the first, between gaz de france and suez, is unnatural because it creates an energy monopoly in belgium in the gas and electricity sectors and further closes the french market to the presence of competitors; the second merger, between enel and suez, could lead to diversification in the french and belgian energy markets. the principle of reciprocity in relations between european countries in the energy sector is essential for a european energy market serving consumers and for a common european energy policy. in italy, large space has been given to energy companies from other countries through privatisation and liberalisation policies. this has also happened in other european nations. the french violation of the principle of reciprocity in this case is not justified by the need to guarantee energy autonomy through national samples, but is instead an expression of a policy of excessive nationalism: france already has its national energy champions, it does not need to create new ones. the merger between gaz de france and suez, which controls the belgian electrabel, would pose a serious risk of encouraging protectionist tendencies not only in the energy sector but also in other industrial, financial and service sectors. the european commission has in other cases used its antitrust instruments to a severe degree to block the development of dominant positions and the retaliation of international competition. this has recently happened in the abn-amro/bank antonveneta and bbva/banque nationale du travail cases, which now appear to have benefited bnp paribas, a french bank. it is desirable that the commission should apply the same rigor to the free movement of capital. even in these circumstances the principle must apply to everyone.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the process of industrial and financial concentration can strengthen the european union in the world. in some cases and at certain stages it can be carried out in a useful way by national means, but these are often defensive and risk triggering a dangerous protectionist spiral which must be stopped: the legal framework must be further developed, the national rules on acquisitions and mergers must be brought closer together, otherwise the pursuit of reciprocity clauses will crush all countries on the most closed and protective norm. finally, in some sectors we will inevitably have oligopolistic structures, for example in energy. these arrangements must not be collusive or unfavourable to consumers and public control of certain companies must not lead to easy market abuse. in short, we need more strength and more integration for the regulatory authority, more strength for antitrust and, immediately, a more active and more decisive attitude on the part of the commission.

member of the commission. mr president, i want to start by thanking mr graefe zu baringdorf and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for all the work they have carried out on both reports, the first on protection of geographical indications and designations of origin and the second on traditional specialities guaranteed. the commission appreciates the efficient organisation of your work, which has enabled adoption of the reports within a short period of time. in my opening statement i address both reports, thereby focusing on the general background that has led to these commission proposals. firstly, as regards the report on the protection of geographical indications and designations of origin, almost 14 years ago the european community established a voluntary system of geographical indications for agricultural products and foodstuffs other than wines and spirits. since 1993, over 700 names have been registered. almost 300 requests are currently waiting for registration; this gives an idea of the success of this system. this success may explain the interest shown by our trade partners in this regulation. the conclusions of the recent wto panels on cases brought by the us and australia impose on us the obligation to open the community scheme to direct applications and objections from individuals in third countries. this is the fundamental reason for the proposal you have on the table: to ensure conformity with the conclusions of the panels. on the basis of experience gained in managing the registration process, we realised that the current system would not survive an additional burden of direct applications from operators in third countries. thus we had to streamline the system and make it more efficient. if we simply conform to wto rules without increasing the efficiency of the functioning of the system, the whole approval process could come to a standstill. i should add that, in order to avoid any risk of a new complaint at wto level, the procedure for third-country and eu denominations should be as similar as possible. we have all been surprised by the extent of the changes required under the wto ruling. while the community won the panel on the substantive trademark issue, we lost on the procedural questions. we also included one clear policy change, namely promoting the use of community logos for enhancing the credibility of the system. apart from that, however, there are no policy initiatives, as the primary purpose of the proposal is to conform to the wto panel findings within the deadline. the many demands and suggestions for policy development set out in the amendments adopted in the committee on agriculture and rural development are issues that deserve more time to be adequately addressed. let me turn now to the other proposal, which concerns traditional specialities guaranteed. in spite of the modest number of products registered, some producers have shown their interest in this regulation. there are only 50 names registered as traditional specialities guaranteed, but there are 19 applications pending at community level and a number of others under examination in the member states. this regulation has not been amended since its adoption in 1992. the procedures have been designed neither for 25 nor for 27 member states, or for handling a significant number of applications. there is a similar need to streamline and standardise the content of applications so that more efficient procedures are adopted and so that producers who make the effort to engage in quality schemes are not disappointed by approvals being delayed for several years. i also consider it important to correct a number of inconsistencies and to reflect substantial advances in legal drafting standards since 1992. at the same time, we propose simplifications and clarifications and other improvements identical to those proposed for geographical indications and designations of origin. finally, we are keen to make it clear in this regulation that wto rules are respected and to forestall any criticism. in conclusion, these proposals achieve wto conformity and introduce limited but necessary housekeeping that is designed to streamline and clarify procedures. we can thereby underpin the mechanisms and better serve producers and consumers who rely on denominations. however, particularly in the light of the wto deadline of 3 april 2006, we did not propose deeper policy changes. those will be addressed in due course within the framework of a wide reflection on agricultural quality policy.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, "you'll eat when you're competitive" is the slogan of a poster: in the background, a skinny african boy. the phrase is emphatic, but it does sound as if the european union is, and this is an understatement, overestimating the effectiveness of trade in fighting poverty. the report under discussion today is a very weak one, as it contained some points in which the effects of liberalization on the economies of the developing countries were called into question. several econometric studies, a report by christian aid, sandra polanski's winners and losers study, published last week, have shown that many developing countries, especially in sub-saharan africa, would be better off today if we had not introduced wild liberalization measures. polanski's study, which analyses the winners and losers of the liberalizations launched with the doha cycle, confirms data that had already been disseminated by unctad and undp and reaches some conclusions: developing countries are likely to be the losers, as they lack the agricultural and industrial capacity to compete with the rich countries; the winners will be the rich countries: the united states, europe and japan, but also china. free trade will produce modest gains globally, partly because the adjustment costs that countries face when engaging in the liberalization process promoted by the industrialized countries may outweigh the benefits. it is not that we are against trade, but that the opening up of markets can be an effective tool in the fight against poverty, but like any tool it must be used with great caution. first of all, the countries must be enabled to meet their own internal needs by strengthening their productive capacity, in particular in the light of internal food sovereignty objectives, and then it must be possible to cope with competition and supply constraints by providing adequate resources which are not present at present in the financial perspectives. secondly, we must work on the basis of realistic timetables, taking into account the time required for structural adjustment, and thirdly, we must limit the opening of the market, including mechanisms to suspend the process of liberalization if necessary and giving the acp countries the opportunity to protect their nascent and strategic industries. we have used this criterion ourselves for the last century, and some people are actually still trying to use it today. these principles are almost present in the report, partly because these are the demands of the acp countries, they are the ones who formulate them. because an effective principle of partnership requires that we take account of the demands of our partners, especially if they are justified, especially if they are supported by civil society in europe and the acp countries. the economic partnership agreements are also, and above all, because they are based on the legal and institutional framework of the cotonou agreement, which was signed by the european union, and their ultimate objective is development and the fight against poverty. the same principle of partnership does not give us the right to impose agreements. i believe that they should do so and one of the main points of the report is the request to the commission to study immediately the alternatives so that the acp countries can, after assessing the options, choose whether to sign these agreements or not. the reciprocity with which liberalization is being demanded means applying equal laws to persons who are not economically and developmentally equal. that does not bring equality and democracy at all. thinking of development in terms of just the increase in gross domestic product in a country is very reductive. development is difficult to define, but when my report asks the commission to protect the water, health and education sectors from liberalisation, it is essentially about rights that must be guaranteed, as when the cape town declaration is cited, the acp-eu joint assembly also has the competence to set development indicators to assess the achievement of results and trade negotiations, calling for social and environmental indicators such as the creation of decent work, health, education, gender equality to be included. it is about rights, the same rights for which we in europe have fought, the same values on which the european union is founded. the european parliament cannot wish to erase these values. we are at a crucial moment in the fight against poverty, and we must also respond to the objectives we have set ourselves.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking mrs morgantini for her excellent work. in a society now dominated by a globalised economic market, the promotion of development cooperation is a duty for the community institutions, in a world context in which three billion people live on less than two dollars a day and over one billion survive on one dollar. the community's policy on the environment is based on the principle of subsidiarity, and the community's policy on the environment is based on the principle of subsidiarity. the union's cooperation policies must include priorities aimed at transforming the internal processes in these countries, promoting a stable, open and democratic political climate and an increase in welfare. in this context, it can be said that the economic partnership agreements represent an appropriate means of strengthening and implementing acp-eu trade relations. we must also stress another point: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union. we must always remember that effective integration and economic growth, if it is to succeed and have a positive impact on the social fabric of developing countries, must necessarily be accompanied by an improvement in the general living conditions of the population. in this context, a precise, concrete and consistent commitment is needed.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the morgantini report is an important attempt to limit the damage caused by the epas. do you really think that to reduce and eradicate hunger and poverty you need a free trade agreement? consider the case of burundi: the theoretical abolition of tariffs, as envisaged by the epas, would allow the european union to gain a share of trade of usd 12.4 million, which burundi would lose, after having already calculated the gain of local consumers. this is shown by a study by the economic commission for africa, a un organization, which also highlighted that the continent already has a very high share of wealth owned by residents abroad, more than any other region in the world: that's a whopping 39%. the idea that further expansion of liberalism can produce wealth in those areas is also refuted by the data on subsidies. in nigeria, the cheapest meat is german and english, and in senegal, 52,000 tons of onions exported from the netherlands in 2005 alone have put farmers in a very difficult situation. the epas were originally conceived in the framework of the cotonou agreement, which specifically stipulates the fight against poverty and social development, but instead have become something that does not promote social development, but further poverty.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am particularly pleased to be speaking today, not as the usual representative of my group, but as the rapporteur for the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights, which represents a larger majority. as such, i would like to make a few points about this report, the main purpose of which is to stress that the question of the application of community law is as much an important part of the better regulation dossier as the other issues we will be discussing this afternoon. the commission's report is very clear on this point. there are very serious problems, particularly in environmental legislation, but also in legislation relating to the internal market, and the responsibility is, needless to say, primarily with the member states. the responsibility for non-application, however, is also due to a procedure which, being provided for in the treaties, is not easy to improve. this is a slow procedure with relatively insufficient penalties: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the community. i would like to know whether you consider this question of the application of community law to be a priority for the commission or not. i do not think that is the case from the point of view of communication, because, as we know, the issue of withdrawal and amendment of directives is given more priority than their proper application. i believe that there are basically two schools of thought in the commission: one that says: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. "we try instead to apply the rules as they are, not in a rigid way, but in a positive way, taking into account procedures that are as fast and lawful as possible". i would like to give a few examples: we believe that a number of decisions taken by the commission in connection with the opening of certain procedures, such as those on gmos in austria, were particularly swift and particularly well done, whereas, on the other hand, as regards france and its failure to apply the natura 2000 directive, we have been waiting for three years for the commission to take action under article 228, or the article on fines, after the ruling of the court of justice. similarly, there are interesting situations with regard to the right of citizens to reimbursement of their medical expenses. we know that this issue, which is of great importance to the citizens themselves, is unresolved because it is a politically complicated problem to deal with. at the same time, article 228 was invoked in only two cases: in the case of the greek landfills, which was suspended after a very short time, and in the case of the spanish bathing waters, which was withdrawn at the last minute because of a matter which the commission itself recognises as being quite doubtful from a legal point of view. what response do we give or what proposals do we put forward to resolve a situation where we think the commission should act in a more transparent way? first of all, we believe that there should be better evaluation and better transparency in the way the law is applied. i think it is important that the commission should send us its compliance studies on the application of the law, which we have unfortunately not been able to do. secondly, i think it is very important to have a transfer of resources from all those who will no longer be legislators to those who will be enforcers. we do not agree, for example, with the idea that this transfer should be made to those who will be dealing with impact assessments, which is something that is being discussed in the commission at the moment, and thirdly - and this concerns us - we believe that the european parliament should intervene much more precisely on the subject of the application of community law, not to touch the commission's powers - i know that this is a very worrying subject for the members of this institution - but, on the contrary, to get, as the committee on the environment and other committees do, a more precise idea of what is happening. i believe that the name and shame policy, also in the application of community law, is very useful and that the commission, perhaps, should help us to apply it more decisively.

author of the book. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are again discussing, as we have done on several occasions in this parliament, a very sensitive issue, which concerns immunity. i am honoured to have the opportunity, on behalf of the committee and the coordinators of the legal affairs committee, to reopen the debate with my question. i think all members are aware of the need for common european parliament rules on immunity, this is a historic aspiration of the european parliament. twenty years ago a colleague of ours, mr donnez, had a report on european parliamentary immunity adopted in order to overcome a situation which was already limited, inadequate for the breathing of the european parliament as a whole, twenty years ago. the protocol on privileges and immunities provided for the immunity of the member of the european parliament from censure in the expressions used in votes, but at the same time referred to the member's national legislation to establish the rules on immunity. of course, there was a logic to all this and at that time, since parliament was then an assembly of the various national parliaments, the rule had its own ratios, its own justification. but today it is clear that thanks to universal suffrage, with all the gains made in the meantime, while parliament has not remained inert, there is a case law, there is a certain attitude on the part of the legal affairs committee, which also in the previous legislature formulated and supported a different demand, namely that all members of the european parliament must have a common statutory reference, a common organizational reference. it is clear not only to the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights but to parliament as a whole that it is difficult for members to refer to national legislation: england has a law of a certain kind, germany has another, italy had another, then it changed it. this does not enhance the prestige of the european parliament and does not lead to its effective autonomy or independence. after much discussion, you too, mr president, who is currently presiding over this house, will be well aware of this, since we have discussed and approved the statute of the european parliamentarian in the legal affairs committee and twice in this house. the council, however, took the view that this was a matter of primary law, so we amended the part of the statute which dealt with the organization of the assembly. a difficult management followed, which then led to a result: the council, ladies and gentlemen, mr president, has endeavoured to convene an intergovernmental meeting of the states, of all the various countries, in order to ratify what we decided in this house. i think we have now reached a very important point of balance: we have discussed and we have given the european parliament as a whole, with great foresight, prerogatives which enhance the role of the parliament and strengthen its independence. of course, since the council's commitment dates back to may 2005 and we are practically in may 2006, we have asked this question to urge a swift conclusion. if our colleague mr donnez felt this need 20 years ago, as parliament's vote has shown, it is still important and fundamental, and the council must immediately ratify what we have decided and established. we have made a great leap forward, and when it above all our role. the council is being urged to do this, and i hope that parliament as a whole will take this urge into account and that every group, every member, even an individual, will share it, the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the european parliament has the important task of granting discharge for the implementation of the 2004 budget to 14 european agencies which receive total, partial or indirect subsidies from the european union. i shall not dwell here on the specific features and problems of each agency, but will merely highlight the elements which have emerged as the main points of common discussion. i take this opportunity to emphasize what i have just said, namely that the discharge is being made on only 14 agencies compared to the 27 existing ones. i wonder how many of you are actually aware of the number and the actual functions of these bodies. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is not for nothing that, after the discussion of my report in committee, a study was commissioned, and is still under way, to analyse and clarify the situations of the european agencies. the study is highlighting what the report has already pointed out, namely the lack of harmonisation between the different agencies and the risk of lack of transparency linked to the difficulties of control by parliament. to this end, i asked the council in the report to open negotiations as soon as possible on the conclusion of the proposal for an interinstitutional agreement, which was presented by the commission at the request of parliament, which in its 2003 discharge report on the agencies asked for the institutional agreement to be opened in order to bring all the agencies into a common regulatory framework. i would like to stress the unfairness of the present situation with regard to parliament's powers of discharge, pointing out that under article 185 of the financial regulation parliament grants discharge for the implementation of the budget to bodies set up by the community which have legal personality and which actually receive subsidies from the budget. in fact, it is important to note that not all these bodies are fully or even partially financed through budgetary grants, so it can be concluded that the discharge decision concerns both budgetary financing and other forms of financing of these bodies. the situation is clearly unacceptable and implies that some bodies set up by the union must be accountable for the way they spend funds from different budgetary sources, while others, which do not receive the subsidy from the budget, are not required to do so. an amendment to the financial regulation which i proposed and which was approved by the committee on budgetary control introduced exactly this principle: if the amended regulation is adopted, parliament's powers of control will be greatly expanded in the years to come, in line with the principles of transparency and democracy. in the course of the report, the court of auditors' analyses have been of great help, as they have revealed some very minor irregularities, and i therefore agree with the court of auditors' opinion, which proposed that the directors of all 14 agencies analysed should be discharged. it regrets, however, that the analysis requested of the court is purely technical in nature, and that no control is carried out on the way the budget allocated has been spent in the current year. i have made this point in the working document accompanying the reports. proposing that the court of auditors should, in the years to come, supplement the present evaluation with an audit of the quality of services, skills and activities, or the efficiency of the way the budget is spent by the individual agencies. many of the problems identified are recurrent and so we speak of a horizontal analysis of the problems that have emerged at the horizontal level with respect to the various agencies: one of these problems concerns the financial regulation, which was designed for the agencies, while the subsequent financial regulations specific to each agency were designed to follow as closely as possible the general financial regulation created for the commission. this is a generally valid criterion, but it is sometimes not appropriate for smaller agencies, which will need to be reformed. this is one of the main objections raised by the court of auditors. the problems of staff selection are also common to several agencies; as agencies certainly need more assistance than larger institutions; i therefore think it is important that the commission should make available to them the services offered by epso, the commission's directorate-general for personnel selection, as well as other horizontal services such as training and legal services. another problem concerns internal auditing, which is too burdensome for some agencies; i therefore think it is useful for the commission to present a report on the current situation, describing both the internal audit capabilities that exist in each agency and the internal audit services that the commission is able to make available to smaller agencies. finally, i would like to focus on a matter which has been the subject of intense debate and has given rise to divergent thinking between parliament and the commission, namely the question of the european agency for reconstruction, which was set up in 2000 to provide assistance for the reconstruction, development and stability of the regions of kosovo, serbia, montenegro and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia through the cards programme. as the programme has come to an end, the commission has taken the decision to close the agency by 2008. in view of the excellent work done in recent years and in order to avoid the loss of valuable experience gained over many years of activity, i proposed in my report to extend the mandate of the agency so that it can be used to provide reconstruction assistance wherever it is needed, for example in iraq, afghanistan, pakistan or even in countries that have recently been affected by the tsunami, in order to complement the humanitarian first aid provided by echo, the commission department created to provide aid in the event of natural disasters or armed conflicts in territories outside the union. i think that is about all that was said on the report, which i hope will be voted on at the next plenary session.
