the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on the eve of the vote on the report on food labelling, i am pleased to inform the house that after intensive negotiations we have reached a common text which i hope will enable us to avoid the conciliation procedure. before going into detail, i should like to thank the shadow rapporteurs of the other groups, mr sommer, mr corbey, mr maaten, mr evans, mr breyer, mr liotard and mr blokland, for their decisive contribution and for their readiness to dialogue, even in the most difficult moments. in a situation of deadlock, in which the council seemed to have given us nothing more, we were able to draw up a compromise package: the council has adopted a final text which, with the agreement of all the parliamentary groups, led the council to accept the proposals. the only thing missing is the seal of tomorrow's vote and i would therefore ask all members to support the compromise in order to achieve the qualified majority needed to amend the common position. i think that, on the whole, it is a balanced text which effectively pursues the objective of ensuring that the consumer is given correct, transparent and comprehensible information, so that he can make a balanced and informed choice of his diet. we all agree in this house that we must promote a healthy and balanced diet for the citizens of europe and that we must avoid that a tempting label promising extraordinary benefits for the consumer's health or, even worse, for his health, is actually a high-calorie food, without the consumer being able to identify it as such. in a europe where, according to the who, one in five children is obese, and in the light of recent studies showing the link between advertising and the consumption of junk food, this regulatory intervention is now untenable. i believe that the primary objective of consumer protection has been fully achieved in the text resulting from the compromise. i would add that, through parliament's intervention, we have been able to respond to the requests for clarity and certainty of timing that the food industry has been concerned about. it was not a simple compromise, partly because on some points the council's position remained very rigid - almost unshakable - until the end of the negotiations. i therefore consider it a great success that we have obtained concessions on these points: i refer in particular to article 4 and the measures on alcohol which we shall deal with later. but i would like to stress at this point that the agreement with the council is a package which must be supported in its entirety. i therefore urge that amendments nos 90 and 49 be rejected immediately, since they are outside the package agreed with the other european institutions. as regards the introduction of so-called 'health' labels on the market, the council agreed to introduce a simplified and faster procedure which will give our companies greater certainty. it was clear from our unanimous vote in the committee on the environment that the shortening of the time should not be at the expense of careful scientific checks on the veracity of the statements on the labels. the european food safety authority (efsa) was to have exactly the same time period to check the claims in both procedures. the council followed us in this proposal and, as a final result, parliament has succeeded in obtaining, within eight months, final authorization for the placing on the market of health labels which do not present any particular difficulties. on the other hand, for some labels which are particularly dangerous because they are highly suggestive, such as those which claim to reduce health risks and those which relate to children's development, the simplified procedure will not be applicable. on the contrary, these labels will have to be subject to the full authorisation procedure which ensures greater scientific control not only by efsa and the commission but also by the member states in the framework of the comitology procedure. on the controversial subject of nutritional profiles, the famous article 4, i would like to remind you that until last wednesday the council was opposed to any derogation from the text. in essence, according to the common position, no type of labelling nutritional or health could be used on a product that did not comply with the nutritional profiles established by efsa. for example, a candy with a high sugar content could never have contained a health or nutritional claim. the compromise text, accepted by all the groups and the council, now provides for the possibility of labelling nutritionally, even when a substance exceeds the nutritional profile, provided that a warning to the consumer of a high presence of the substance exceeding the nutritional profiles is added on the same side of the package. this ensures that the consumer is given correct information, which is readily available on the same side of the packaging, while leaving the industry free to use this type of claim. i regard this text as a victory for parliament on a point which the council initially considered untouchable. as regards trade marks, we have obtained that for 15 years existing trade marks can continue to be used without further requirements. after expiry of the time limit, they may continue to be used provided that they are accompanied by a corresponding claim which complies with the provisions of this regulation. i think that this is a sufficiently long transitional period for industry, but one which will allow it to adapt to community rules. in addition, we have preserved the use of generic names that traditionally accompany food products such as "appetizer", "digestive" and "cough drops": the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used effectively. i would also remind the house that all negative labelling systems, the so-called red lights or red flags, which are already in use in some countries, are outside the scope of the regulation and will therefore be regulated at national level. as a parliament we have achieved important victories in the negotiations on the protection of smes. what was initially said to be technically impossible has now been granted. the commission notes that the aid is limited to the minimum necessary to ensure that the aid is compatible with the internal market. under the new article 15, the commission will have to commit itself to making available tools and guidelines directed at smes in order to facilitate in particular the application of this regulation. in addition, by reducing the data protection period to five years, from the seven originally envisaged, we have shortened the time for access to the use of claims for small and medium-sized enterprises that do not have the financial means to support labelling research on their own. smes will be able to use all the labels already authorised and available on the list provided for in article 13 in advance, thanks to parliament's amendment. the use of the website is free of charge and requires no formalities. even those who cannot afford to finance research on a claim can therefore use it easily and without additional burden. as regards the protection of children - a matter which has been very much discussed in this house - we have obtained that all labels relating to the development or improvement of children's health be assessed through the full authorization procedure, to ensure that the scientific validity of the label and its comprehensibility for the consumer is carefully monitored, including by the member states. the indications of medical associations, dieticians and nutritionists will be accepted as opposed to those of individual doctors. as regards alcohol, nutritional labels were already allowed in the common position. for drinks with more than 1.2% alcohol, labels with the words "reduced alcohol content" or "less calories" were allowed. the council has given us the option of using the term 'low alcohol' as a last resort. we have also received important recognition for the importance of maintaining the different culinary traditions and for the possibility of facilitating the sale of bulk food. in conclusion, i would ask everyone to support the amendments which form part of the compromise signed by all the groups and only those groups, in order to bring to a positive conclusion the legislative process of this report which is so controversial that it has remained in this parliament for more than three years. i would like to thank everyone, including the staff of the groups and the technicians who supported us.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, so-called 'functional' foods, enriched with substances which are supposed to improve the health or well-being of consumers, are one of the most innovative sectors with the greatest scope for market growth. it is therefore necessary to ensure control of this type of food and, above all, control of the statements on the labels, which attract the consumer by promising benefits from a dietary or health point of view. the compromise text ensures transparent and comprehensive information on food labels and allows the consumer to make an informed dietary choice. this is all the more urgent when we consider the impact of advertising on children. advertising directly influences the food preferences of children by changing their eating habits. parliament's intervention also brought due attention to smes, which need support to adapt to the new rules introduced by the regulation and which will therefore be able to count on certain time limits for the placing of their products on the market and the possibility of using the claims already authorised. finally, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs poli bortone, for her excellent and not easy work.

member of the commission. mr ebner refers to the need to protect children and young people from aggressive advertising for ringtones, mobile phones, games, etc. and asks whether the commission intends to take action on this. the recently adopted unfair commercial practices directive bans aggressive commercial practices and gives specific protection to children and young people. if a commercial practice is specifically aimed at a particular group of consumers such as children, its impact will be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. furthermore, the directive bans direct pressure on children to purchase. the distance selling directive also protects consumers who purchase goods and services at a distance, in other words with no face-to-face contact. it includes provisions on prior information. when providing that information, the supplier must have due regard for the protection of minors. the commission has already launched a review of eight of the consumer directives, including the distance selling directive. issues such as those raised by mr ebner will be addressed in the review. a communication on the review will be published this autumn.

the agenda includes the report by mr richard howitt, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, on the annual report on human rights in the world 2005 and the eu's policy on the matter (2005/2203 (ini)) - (a6-0158/2006)
the howitt report is an important step forward in comparison with the past, as it seeks to analyse the impact of the european union's human rights policies, and above all their effectiveness vis-à-vis third countries. the first significant change in this report is the request to include - as from the next annual report - an examination of the actual respect of the democracy clause, which was voted on 14 february. i am sorry to say, however, that neither the council nor the commission has given any precise indication as to how they intend to implement this clause on democracy and rights in trade relations between europe and third countries. the resolution calls for the european union to support the activities of the newly created un human rights council and at the same time calls for universal ratification of the rome statute establishing the international criminal court, in particular by the united states, for which there can be no legal exception. the document also condemns in particular the bilateral agreements which some eu countries have concluded with the us to guarantee the impunity of us soldiers. it also called for the european union to be consistent in its human rights policy, particularly in the case of china, with regard to the tibetan people and guantánamo, and called for the immediate closure of all special prisons. however, i cannot ignore some of the limitations of the report, which makes no reference to the european union's failure to support human rights at the sixth wto ministerial conference in hong kong. the council has not yet adopted a decision on the matter. the commission is also aware of the fact that the council has not yet adopted a decision on the matter. finally, as regards colombia, article 41 is not as explicit as the situation of the citizens of the latin american state deserves, as in the case of the inhabitants of peaceful communities involved in numerous massacres that go unpunished. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances. one last note: although i agree with the request that the european union's annual report on human rights include the involvement of the european parliament, i still believe that it is equally necessary for parliament to continue to draw up its own specific vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to thank all those who have spoken in the debate. i agree with most of the comments i have heard. firstly, this is not a tragic emergency at the world cup, but a modern form of slavery which will unfortunately continue to affect hundreds of thousands and probably millions of young women. it is therefore clear that we must not confine ourselves to the football world cup. for this reason, as i have already said, we will be organising a workshop immediately after the world cup, during which we will be gathering all the experiences of this month and drawing conclusions to draw up a document which will be useful for all other sporting events of this type, but also for cultural or political events. for example, at the hanover expo a few years ago, german police authorities noted an increase in forced prostitution. there's been a lot of talk about the hotlines. in the urgency of giving an answer, and precisely because we believe that ngos should play a role in this project, it was decided to entrust the management of two multilingual helplines, which are already active, to a particularly well-known ngo in germany solvodi which has provided h24 coverage during this period. let me add that, as we have done for the protection of children who are victims of violence, the commission also intends to support the european helplines financially. unfortunately, it was not possible to implement this project under the 2006 budget, but i believe that we will be able to implement it under the 2007 budget. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to support the development of the regions concerned. a lot has been said about communication and information. i fully agree with mr vincenzi when he recommends that we spoil the party if necessary, and therefore avoid silence when there are strong messages to be given. i must admit that we have had a short time and that i have had the institutional need to concentrate on prevention and rapid reaction activities which, of course, will be accompanied by information campaigns. i am also prepared to make a financial contribution to information campaigns on this subject. in addition, as i have already said, we have for the first time activated the network of consulates of the member states in the countries of origin, because we believe that it is in those countries that the information campaign for potential victims must be stronger and more widespread. i certainly agree that the concept of trafficking in human beings and trafficking for sexual exploitation should be separated from the issue of immigration, as these are two totally different issues. you know that we are monitoring the implementation of the european legislation in force, first of all the framework decision, which has to be transposed by the member states and which keeps this matter absolutely separate from the immigration issue. victims are victims, not illegal immigrants, and therefore entitled to benefit from those assistance programmes already provided for in some member states for persons who report that they have been victims of exploitation, or even worse, of forced trafficking for sexual purposes. i also share mr breyer's call for long-term initiatives such as the european day against trafficking in human beings and i hope that by the first half of next year we will be able to set a firm date for this initiative. as i said, i am in favour of reducing demand. however, to know the impact of demand for prostitution on trafficking it is absolutely necessary that analyses are carried out, although some have claimed the opposite. we started working together on this issue earlier this year and i can tell you that we have acquired many new elements. we now know with some precision what the trafficking routes are, we know what the main countries of origin are, we know through which member states of the european union the buses carrying small groups of girls to germany pass. i can also tell you that, although the police figures are difficult to explain, in recent months hundreds of checks have been carried out, not only in germany but also in many transit countries such as poland, hungary and the czech republic, which have led to the arrest and detention of those responsible for trafficking in young women. on the basis of these elements and thanks to the cooperation between the police forces, we were able to reduce the potential impact to a percentage which, however, we are not yet able to determine, because the hundreds of people who were checked and arrested were heading for germany. i would therefore like to express my appreciation for the conduct of the german authorities. mr batzeli asked how the german authorities were working on the ground. i can confirm that they work well, both at federal and at länder level. when you read the final report at the end of the world cup, you will find out what we are also finding out, that the checks have been strengthened and that many cases have been detected where false declarations of short-term stay, for example to work in a bar or to perform domestic work, were actually hiding victims of sexual exploitation. the victims have been identified and the perpetrators have probably been arrested. in conclusion, i would reiterate that the root causes must be tackled. there is a european action plan, which you supported last december, which we must now implement, starting from consideration of the inviolable nature of the human right and dignity of every person. that's what we'll be working on over the next few months.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the adoption of the seventh framework programme was supported by this parliament in the awareness that the challenge for the competitiveness and development of the nations of the entire continent lies in the revival of research opportunities. i think that the financial effort should be stepped up. if 3% of investment in the european union is allocated to research and development by 2010, it may be possible to alleviate the shortage of some 700 000 researchers currently registered in the union. public support for research remains necessary in sensitive areas such as health, energy and the environment, and i think there is a great deal of agreement in this house. however, this support cannot come only from the european institutions. they should instead encourage national governments to increase the financial allocation for research in their budgets and thus improve working conditions in the sector, both in terms of the possibilities for developing public human resources and in terms of promoting private investment and public-private synergies. the problems of research and development are not the same in europe. it is the different working conditions and prospects for young researchers and their transition from academic studies to the world of work. for example, in italy, the relationship between universities and enterprises lacks concrete training and apprenticeship opportunities. the simple exchange of information is also lacking. very low wages and limited research funding lead to emigration or, more often, to abandonment of public research in order to pursue more rewarding personal paths of achievement. i hope that the establishment of a european research council will help to fill the gaps in the national systems. the very high number of amendments tabled to this excellent report by mr buzek is a testimony to the interest and priority which parliament attaches to research for the development of our continent.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall confine myself to the ethical issues. in order to understand these kinds of problems, you first need to understand what we're talking about. firstly, it must be remembered that the question is not whether or not to authorize experimentation on embryos, but whether research projects, which are inevitably destructive, can be financed by the european union, that is to say with money also coming from states which consider the destruction of embryos for experimental purposes to be a serious violation of fundamental rights. secondly, we must consider the foreseeable effects of the research. to date, no therapeutic efficacy has been demonstrated from embryonic stem cells. on the contrary, their carcinogenic effects have been demonstrated in mice. to date, there is not a single publication in the world that demonstrates the therapeutic effects of embryonic stem cells. on the other hand, so-called adult stem cells are already curing many diseases and the prospects are extremely promising, which means that if we really want to save people's health, we must concentrate the few financial resources in the areas where it is easier and faster to achieve the goal than elsewhere. finally, the principle of subsidiarity must be recalled. there are countries where experimentation on embryos calls into question the very concept of human dignity, the very basis of human rights. to admit experimentation on human beings means, in other words, to regard the human being as a thing and not as a human being. it is not a question of labelling, tourism or town planning, but of the very foundation of human rights as conceived, perhaps wrongly, by one state in the place of another. i therefore believe that it is not right that the states which allow embryo testing should be able to impose on the states which do not allow it that they should contribute their money to carrying out the testing in other countries.
those who oppose the use of human embryos for research purposes are in favour of the life and dignity of the human being, because they defend the existence of an embryo which is biologically inclined to life, but which in the specific cases to which reference is made would not see this opportunity because it is destined for destruction. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval, and the council will be consulted on the matter. it is important to give a signal of openness to research, in the name of the right of every individual to enjoy the best possible conditions of physical and mental health and to take advantage of the extraordinary advances that science can offer. it is right, however, to restrict indiscriminate research (reproductive cloning, chimeras, the creation of embryos specifically for research purposes, etc.) and to check its morality, just as it is right to respect the will of the citizens in member states where ethical questions prevail over progress. for the rest, limiting our possibilities means taking away from many the hope of a better future.

patentability. earlier this year, the commission’s directorate-general for the internal market and services launched a broad consultation of all interested parties on the future patent policy in europe, with a particular focus on the structure of the european patent system. the deadline for the consultation was 12 april 2006, and preliminary findings will be discussed with stakeholders at the hearing in brussels on 12 july 2006. consultation is intended to ensure that any further possible action in the area of eu patents policy takes account of all stakeholders’ needs without discrimination. parliament will be duly informed of the results of this consultation. one of the options presented to stakeholders refers to the commission’s proposal for community patent regulation. software as such. moreover, the new jurisdiction of the european court of justice would improve the safeguards against the grant of patents in error to a computer program. therefore, the commission the commission's vice-president ladies and gentlemen, we have before us a draft legislation which the commission and the european parliament consider to be an important initiative. the proposal adopted by the commission on 22 september 2005 is important because the fight against the terrorist threat on all fronts remains a priority and because we need to learn the lessons from the application of the legislation in force. we must continue to look for ways to improve the protection of european citizens and to better reconcile the security requirements with the operational needs of all actors, public authorities, airports and airlines. the legislation in force establishes rules in the field of civil aviation safety. it was drafted in the most urgent of circumstances following the attacks of september 11, 2001. the project aims to consolidate this legislation in the light of experience. the rules in force are relatively detailed, as is evident when attempts are made to introduce new technologies or to make the system more flexible to deal with real risks. with experience, a need for simplification is felt. without calling into question the principle of subsidiarity, the commission believes that harmonisation of safety requirements is essential in the european union and that it is in the interests of european civil aviation that this harmonisation be strengthened. we must live up to that expectation. experience gained through inspections carried out by the commission has shown that certain provisions of the regulation need further clarification. the commission has proposed a rebalancing of its implementing powers in the comitology procedure to allow it to react more rapidly to technological developments and to strengthen the confidentiality of rules which should not be in the public domain. i am convinced that this revised text on aviation safety, if adopted, will not only strengthen the protection of citizens but also establish a consolidated framework which strikes a good balance between the risks of the extension of controls and their operational impact, with the respect of all parties. i am pleased to note that the draft report before us today takes up the reasoning behind the commission's initiative, but also the practical operational requirements that have emerged. mr costa has done a very valuable job and i would like to thank considers the role of women to be important, acknowledges the difficulties they face in operating in this sector, recalls the issue of safety on board, stresses the importance of vocational training the economic and social crisis affecting the italian fisheries sector, which has been hit by operating costs of over 40% and income losses of around 25% over the last three years, is affecting the least competitive segments of the fleet, in particular coastal fishing, which is more affected by the high volatility of fuel costs and the increase in variable costs. in addition to the economic difficulties, the coastal fisheries sector is faced with the lack of a specific regulatory framework. the european union must adopt a realistic approach and allow for the adoption of definitions that are not too rigid. in the future mediterranean regulation, for example, it will be appropriate to provide for the possibility of proposing adjustments at national level. the commission must recognise the specific nature of small-scale coastal fishing and artisanal fishing within the common fisheries policy, taking into account the fact that certain coastal areas, in particular island or outermost regions, are heavily dependent on fishing and the industries generated by it. it should analyse the extent to which existing instruments are adequate to meet the needs of the sector by involving more representatives of the sector in the decision-making process.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am answering both questions at the same time, concerning the use of wood chips in wine production. the purpose of the draft commission regulation, which is being examined by the wine steering committee, is to lay down the conditions for the use of oak wood chips in the production of wine. this new oenological process was decided by the council in regulation (ec) no 2165/2005 of 20 december 2005. the commission considers that the provisions on wine labelling contained in this proposal meet the requirements of transparency for consumers and the requirements of product quality. the proposal lays down rules on wine labelling to avoid misleading consumers. however, the possibility of using the term 'oak cask' or 'oak barrel' for wines which have been aged or matured in wooden vessels and which have never been in contact with pieces of oak wood is retained. under these conditions, wines aged in contact with pieces of oak wood and showing the taste of wine aged in contact with wood cannot be confused with wines aged in the traditional manner in barrel barrels and therefore no specific indication is required for these wines. under regulation (ec) no 1493/1999 on the common organisation of the market in wine, member states may impose stricter conditions on oenological practices for quality wines from specified growing regions and for table wines with a geographical indication in order to ensure that the essential characteristics of those quality wines are preserved. the commission cannot interfere with those national powers. for the union producers, this procedure has now been approved by the council. and the international wine organization has already approved it a few years ago. the commission considers that the traditional barrel ageing methods will be maintained for producers of high quality wines, as is the case in third countries which have allowed this practice for years. long-term use in producing third countries and numerous trials carried out under the control of the european union show that the procedure does not have negative consequences for the health of consumers. the commission considers that greater flexibility in authorising new oenological practices will allow community producers to expand their market and reach more consumers, in particular for export, and will improve the competitiveness of the wine sector vis-à-vis third countries.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with today's decision europe has decided to invest in a cohesion policy with great prospects, allocating eur 308 billion to the objectives of convergence, social cohesion and the promotion of territorial cohesion. in the european union of 25, 123 million people, or 27% of the total population, live in regions with a per capita gdp of less than 75% of the community average; two-fifths of these live in regions belonging to the old member states. cohesion policy helps to share the benefits of european economic development by anticipating change and helping areas in difficulty, often for structural or geographical reasons. this cohesion policy helps to limit the negative effects of globalisation. the recent reform of the structural funds, which are essential instruments of cohesion policy, which introduces greater efficiency, transparency and accountability, can only be welcomed. the management system has been simplified by introducing differentiation and proportionality in the context of sound financial management, in response to the requests for simplification from the main actors of cohesion policy: the member states. the new reform is based on the priorities of lisbon and gothenburg: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling of foodstuffs. it has been decided to invest in human capital, innovation and the promotion of the knowledge society, entrepreneurship, environmental protection and more. the new objectives are numerous, and include the creation of three new objectives: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation of the regions in the community, such as reducing the number of structural funds, strengthening the partnership, increasing financial resources for islands and regions with geographical handicaps and protecting the phasing-out regions which will soon no longer be eligible for the convergence objective.
the regions are the building blocks of europe, and cultural diversity and the promotion of the different regional realities are among the union's main characteristics. i am therefore pleased that more than one third of the union budget has been allocated to the structural funds for the new period 2007-13. sustaining regional identity while pursuing convergence at european level in terms of development and improving the conditions for growth and employment is in fact an essential condition for achieving the lisbon objectives and promoting the economy, especially at local and regional level. in fact, it is the small businesses that drive the market in europe, and the idea of strengthening competitiveness and involvement at this level, by promoting partnerships between public, private and non-governmental actors operating at the territorial level, can only encourage an economic recovery that would benefit the union in its global context. i hope that the regions will rise to the challenge and turn the guidance and resources provided by these institutions into concrete plans for economic and social development, focusing above all on full employment and the intelligent and sustainable exploitation of the human, artistic and natural resources they have at their disposal in large quantities and of high quality.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the issues raised in the commissioner's communication are very important. in the face of the changes which have taken place and are still taking place in the national and european production systems, europe is faced with the problem of managing industrial restructuring processes, which have had a very heavy impact on workers and on the various territories. mr harbour asked a moment ago what the theme of the future might be, and my answer is this: "the theme of the future is how to govern these processes". the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the problem of unemployment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full, and i am sure that the commission will take the necessary steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. this is why we must adopt a clear european approach, based on the idea of effective governance of these processes, and also to give greater coherence to the lisbon objectives themselves and to the social dialogue itself, which is considered one of the pillars of this strategy. the call is therefore to find a common position to give strength and substance to the action of the european institutions themselves, starting with parliament, in this field. i would like to stress one last point. it is now quite clear that the restructuring issue requires a review of the community instruments available. just one example - and i would like to hear the commissioner's opinion on this - if we are to really govern these processes, there is an inescapable need to strengthen and reform european works councils. the directive needs to be updated if we are to meet the new requirements in this area. i hope that there will be a common position on this from the whole of parliament and from the commission.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mrs del castillo, on her report. i would like to address two issues: the commission has also adopted a communication on the future of the european research area and the sme theme. building the european research area means building the single market of the most valuable commodity: knowledge. we must therefore devote to its construction the same determination that europe as a whole has devoted to the achievement of monetary union and the single market for other goods. in a few months we will be launching the seventh framework programme and the union still has a very, very diverse landscape of national and regional systems for research and innovation and, as a result, there is no teamwork. this is at the expense of systematic cooperation and efficiency. if we are to achieve lisbon, all the actors involved, public and private, at regional, national and community level, will have to make their own contribution through synergistic and complementary actions, developing systems as well as policies that are coherent and mutually compatible. as far as small and mediumsized enterprises are concerned, the fall in productivity and thus in the competitiveness of the italian economy is attributed by several sources to the fact that there is little innovation in italy. this is because many italian firms feel that new technologies are essentially useless or superfluous. this negative phenomenon is linked to the small size of our enterprises, which on average employ about four people; but if the phenomenon is particularly serious in my country, it also affects a large part of europe. i therefore propose that, in addition to the various measures to support small and mediumsized enterprises, which are provided for in the castillo report - which i fully support - training measures be introduced specifically for small entrepreneurs so that they understand that innovation has become a necessity for survival. finally, i would urge the member states and regions, while recognising research and innovation as a top priority, not to waste too much time in the transposition procedures and in the start of implementation of the various programmes and actions, because time for innovation is precious.

, member of the commission. mr president, i should like to start by saying that this commission and i, as commissioner for trade, are fully committed to working very closely with parliament, in line with the framework agreement governing relations between the two institutions. as this question rightly points out, the legal basis for this measure – article 133 of the ec treaty – does not provide specifically for consultation of the european parliament on this proposal for an ‘origin marking’ scheme. however, in line with our commitment to keep the european parliament fully informed, on a par with the council, of the conduct and conclusion of international negotiations, as well as legislative initiatives, the proposal and the accompanying impact assessment were transmitted on 12 january 2006 to the european parliament via the committee on international trade. i should like to refer to paragraph 2 of the motion for a resolution that you have before you. the language of that paragraph is slightly unfortunate because it could, as it is written at the moment, be read as if the commission had not sent any document at all on ‘origin marking’ to parliament. as i said, we sent it as an article 133 document to the inta committee. i believe that it would certainly be fairer to me and to the commission – and more accurate – if an adjustment were made to the wording. our intention has been, and continues to be, to act in line with both the letter and the spirit of the framework agreement. to meet the commitment in that agreement, and in addition to the many formal and informal contacts that i have with you, the commission tries hard to share a maximum of information with parliament, just as i did last week in geneva. in particular we sent to the inta committee copies of all policy documents that are being discussed in the council’s 133 committee. if a more formal interinstitutional way to bring this issue to your attention should have been used on that occasion, the opportunity was certainly not missed on purpose. i very much welcome the interest you have already shown in this proposal through several questions on the subject, which we have answered. so let me now come to our proposal. we have proposed a mandatory origin marking scheme, to create transparency about the origin of certain imported goods according to a single standard by which origin is determined. this system will allow consumers to take informed decisions; it will reduce the incidence of fraudulent or misleading origin marking. we believe it will help improve the image of european goods and will help our competitiveness. while it is clear that ‘made in’ marking as such does not contain information on the social, labour or environmental conditions in the country of production, origin information helps the consumer to choose between different available alternatives according to their preferences and the background information they already have. as regards wto compatibility, the commission believes its proposal is in line with international rules, notably article 9 of the gatt. that provides that wto members may adopt and enforce laws and regulations relating to marks of origin on imports, notably to protect consumers against fraudulent or misleading indications. concerning the enforcement of the proposal, the commission considers that customs authorities are well placed to ensure that the requirements of the proposed scheme are respected, just as they do with many other rules on environmental, health and technical issues. that part of customs work is crucial to ensuring that our businesses can trade on a level playing field and that consumers draw the full benefits of globalisation. i should add that in addition to possible controls carried out before the products are released into the internal market, the regulation provides for member states to check origin marking on goods that are already on the market. that should enable member states to draw on other expertise in policing the scheme, for example by working with those who are presently involved in the enforcement of national rules concerning the voluntary use of origin marking. as you will be aware, mr president, the commission proposal is being debated in the council and i am of course ready to keep you informed as discussions on the proposal move forward.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the compulsory indication of the mark of origin proposed by the commission must be accepted because it has a twofold purpose: the commission's proposal is to inform the consumer more and to make the most of the industrial system of those european countries which are investing large resources in innovation in order to convert their production systems to excellence. we must seek to restore a minimum of equality of rules with those trading areas, china, the united states, canada, japan, which have already introduced the 'made in' system, knowing that this does not entail any risk of illegality. we need a more transparent market and more controls, we need to reduce legal uncertainty and curb counterfeiting and unfair competition. all this can be achieved, directly or indirectly, by making imports 'made in' without additional costs for european producers, exporters and consumers, thus creating a level playing field with trading partners who have already implemented the standard, in line with the political and cultural choice which has been and is intended to create, extend and strengthen an ever larger and freer market in the world. it will also make it possible to develop a quality manufacturing industry, and i emphasize quality, which in many european countries is wrongly considered to be a light industry, which is also a major social issue that europe cannot forget, so that the lisbon objectives are pursued in practice and not with abstract claims. finally, this is an opportunity to put a few questions to the commission. what is the commission's strategy for strengthening the external aspects of european competitiveness, given the very close relationship between industry and trade, between production and promotion? in writing. the indication of the country of origin of a product in the trade mark represents the strength and transparency of the product, a guarantee for the consumer and a duty to defend national work and enterprises. the defence of european products (at least by relying on the clarity of the brands, the production processes and all the guarantees on them which a consumer has a right to know and which, if you will allow, ethics also imposes) is also indispensable to the 'fair competition' which the dominant criteria of the 'free market' (which is therefore free, but correctly competitive) require. the trademark of origin is not in itself a sufficient guarantee of the above, but at least it represents a first step. the compulsory application of the trademark as provided for in the provisions we are discussing here is only a first indispensable measure of defence against those products which are invading the european market, unfairly competing with our products and harming our undertaking and our work. the traceability of a product and, better still, the absolute transparency of the production process, a fair recognition of quality and research and also of the artisanal and industrial tradition of the nations of europe, are also guarantees for the protection of consumers, as well as of european enterprises and industries. that is why i voted for the new regulation, even though i believe it is only a first step.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, with the maastricht treaty the european union became a union of peoples, it acquired its own cultural identity in respect of regional and local differences which, in contrast to an ever-increasing cultural globalisation, constitute the real basic wealth of a common heritage. the island and rural areas are the cradle of this heritage, with their traditions, architecture, local craftsmanship, natural and landscape beauties. it is therefore a matter of priority to protect this enormous heritage, to develop a local development project aimed at activating and encouraging the valorisation of culture and environmental resources, to make them an instrument of growth for an economy that is currently in difficulty. this means first of all an overall improvement of the territory, in which - member of the commission. mr president, once again, i would like to thank mrs prets, the culture committee’s rapporteur, for her commitment and constructive work, including several long meetings with my services and those of the council. for similar reasons, let me also express gratitude to the employment and social affairs committee, and especially the rapporteur, mr kusstatscher. thanks to their political will, flexibility and negotiating skills, we have been able to agree on a reliable compromise text. let me first refer to the main objectives of this proposal from the commission. the aim of the charter is to lay down common principles to make all types of mobility for learning purposes more efficient and more effective. these principles include quality information and guidance for the candidates; a sound learning plan; preparation, especially linguistic preparation; adequate logistical support and mentoring schemes in the host country. we also want to make clear what the responsibilities of all stakeholders are and to ensure fair recognition and evaluation of the study and training on return. we expect the charter to bring significant benefits to users. first, it should help make citizens more confident that mobility is useful and is being carried out in the right conditions. additionally, it should make it easier for the large category of people learning in another country to exercise the right to move and study freely within the european union. it should have a positive impact on the employability of those concerned. indeed, the charter responds to the important components of the social dimension of the european union: mobility, education and training for the acquisition of new skills and employability. i come now to mrs prets’ report, which i welcome very much. i know that the european parliament’s amendments mean that the text now fits even better with the objectives of the proposal. for instance, you point out that mobility is based on common values and on respect for diversity. you have extended the scope of the proposal to the specific needs of disadvantaged groups and people with disabilities. you have invited the commission to encourage the use of a mobility charter by national agencies and other organisations. you have insisted on developing gender-specific statistical data and you have also mentioned the portability of government grants and loans to the host country. to summarise, of the 36 amendments voted by the culture committee, only four have not been accepted by the commission. that was not a refusal of the underlying ideas, however, but only because the matter was outside the scope of the proposal, or else covered by other parts of the text. all the remaining 32 amendments have been fully integrated, either literally or with slight rewording. finally, as you know, coreper last week agreed on the compromise text. not a single member state opposed the text or maintained a reserve. that should ease the agreement in the first reading. therefore, i ask this house to confirm the text in its vote. it should be an excellent conclusion to a most efficient cooperation between institutions. but, before that, i am open to your questions.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, i believe that today marks a significant milestone in the examination of a measure of great importance both to the commission and to parliament. the initiative in question, which was initially adopted in accordance with the formal rules of a procedure which excludes codecision, was subsequently politically reduced to extremely close cooperation with parliament. the trilogue method, which has enabled us to meet many times, is in fact a political solution: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to thank the rapporteurs, mrs gál and mrs kovács, for their fruitful cooperation. we have reached agreement on a number of points and i hope that by the end of this year the few remaining issues will also have been resolved, so that in 2007 - as the european council and parliament have repeatedly said and as the commission itself hopes - the fundamental rights agency will finally be operational. what are the points which still need to be reflected on and deepened, even after the last trilogue, which was also extremely useful? these are the three basic questions which i have recently discussed with the ministers of the interior at the council meeting in luxembourg last week and recently at a meeting with the secretary-general of the council of europe. the first question concerns the relations between the future agency and the council of europe. it is the intention of the commission, my staff and - i am sure - the european parliament itself to avoid any overlap of competences between the new agency and the council of europe, which is already doing exemplary work in the protection and promotion of fundamental rights. i believe that it is possible to pursue the common objective of cooperation between the agency on the one hand and the council of europe on the other, each within its own responsibilities. the agency's primary task is to supervise, monitor and collect data on compliance with community legislation, without going beyond this area of competence. first point then: the council of europe is not a political body, but a political body. the second point concerns the geographical scope of the agency's powers and responsibilities. you will all remember that there was an original position which limited the geographical scope to the member states of the union alone. the need to extend the scope of responsibilities to the applicant countries, countries which are already, albeit to varying degrees, on the way to accession to the european union, was obvious from the outset. the serious problem of the countries in the pre-accession phase, which we call potential candidate countries, has also been raised. this is an extremely important concept, because it refers to a key geographical area for europe: the western balkans. these are countries which are negotiating, in some cases, or applying, in other cases, association and stabilisation agreements with the european union, which touch on, among other things, extremely sensitive matters as regards the protection of fundamental rights. hence the proposal, supported by the council and contained in the text under discussion today, to extend the scope of application to these countries. in this connection, some member states have raised reservations and the council of europe has expressed strong fears, which i have to report. i believe, however, that an appropriate compromise solution can be found, one which does not entirely exclude the prospect of these countries also coming under the agency's jurisdiction. a compromise solution which perhaps takes into account the fact that the agency in question, which will already have all the current responsibilities of the vienna observatory, and therefore racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism, to which new responsibilities will be added, could better concentrate, at least at the outset, on the member states of the european union and the candidate countries. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. this is a point on which there is still room for reflection. the third and final point concerns the inclusion of the so-called 'third pillar' subjects: judicial and police cooperation. the commission - and i personally - have been in favour from the outset of the strategy, which this parliament also considers to be the best, of including this matter in the remit of the agency in question. i think it would be rather difficult to explain to the citizens of europe that we are about to set up an agency to promote and protect fundamental rights, excluding from the scope of these powers the aspects of police cooperation and judicial activity, in respect of which there is an objective need to verify the full and absolute respect of the fundamental rights, for example, of an accused or on trial person. there is also, as you know, a legal basis problem, which i will not deal with at this stage, but for which there is a political motivation. if this agency is to be useful to the citizens, it must include, in some way, the subjects which fall within the scope of the 'third pillar'. it will be up to us to find an acceptable formula, but i do not think it will be to postpone the decision on whether or not to include matters relating to the third pillar until a later stage than the establishment of the agency. to postpone the decision would be to postpone the decision, and that would be wrong in my view. as you know, within the council, some of the major countries of the european union are showing a certain reluctance to accept this inclusion, raising internal constitutional problems. i personally believe that these problems can be overcome and that parliament can play a very important political role in this area. i hope that the council will accept a compromise text which, although not formally adopted in codecision, will represent a joint effort by parliament, the council and the commission. this is perhaps the first time, ladies and gentlemen, that we have, by common political will, abandoned the application of rules which do not allow for the formal codecision procedure, and have in fact reached a joint decision by political means. the agency, which would certainly have a stronger foundation if it had this result behind it, would also be a good example for many other areas, which unfortunately still do not have the codecision procedure.

the commission's vice-president mr president, the commission currently receives fewer complaints about over-reservation than before the increase in compensation rates by regulation no 261/2004. at present, only 8% of complaints received by the commission concerning air passenger rights relate to cases of overbooking or denied boarding, while 60% relate to delays or cancellations. this trend is due, among other things, to the development of low-cost airlines and the increasing use of charter airlines, which do not tend to integrate overbooking into their mode of operation. since the entry into force of this regulation, airlines have been more flexible in seeking volunteers who agree to give up their reservation in exchange for certain agreed benefits. this practice encourages airlines to immediately resolve the problem on the spot. that said, i would like to point out to mr evans that, in accordance with article 17 of the regulation, the commission will present a report to parliament and the council at the beginning of 2007 on the operation and application of this regulation. this communication will be based on a study carried out by an external consultant. a call for tenders has been published for the recruitment of this external consultant. overbooking is one of the points which will be dealt with in this study and the commission will of course wait until it has seen the results of the study before deciding whether or not to adapt the legislation. mr president, if there is one tangible effect of these new regulations on passenger rights, it is the reduction in overbooking, which in some cases - it must be admitted - has become a very harmful habit for passengers.
the commission's vice-president mr titley, it is absolutely essential that we ensure that these passenger rights are respected. i should also say that at the moment i am trying to call on all airports to display passenger rights, so that it is very clear that all passengers must be informed that they cannot be overbooked without being offered in return a significant compensation, as required by the regulation. the three keywords in this area are information, investigation and audit, as i have already indicated. secondly, we shall see whether there is any need to impose sanctions or, at any rate, to take states to the court of justice who have not really monitored the application of these passenger rights. there you go, mr titley. i thank you for this question, which reminds us of the importance of applying european law.

the commission's vice-president mr president, i can confirm that complaints about overbooking have decreased. in 2001, it was over 16%, and today it is 7%. however, i am as convinced as you are that the victims of this practice should turn to the body responsible for examining complaints in each member state. and then, as i said, this audit will give us a much more complete picture of these problems. this will enable us to know which carriers are accustomed to this practice and which ones deserve a serious call to order.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the 2004 annual report on anti-dumping, anti-subsidy and safeguard measures taken by third countries against the community, presented by the commission's services, has revealed a fact which has caused a great deal of concern in our committee. it shows an abnormal increase in cases of trade defence, both by traditional users of such measures and by the more recently developed wto member states. in many cases, wto rules and case law have been partially or totally disregarded, causing injury to the community industry. the main problems for the developed countries, with the united states at the head, are the unilateral application of wto rules, which are not always followed. for some emerging countries, the application of countervailing duties is not intended to combat illegal practices but to provide local industries with additional protection against european imports. in many cases, the investigative standards are low and are such as to raise more than one doubt about their full compliance with wto rules. the commission report lists some of these significant cases, namely the 'zeroing' case with the usa, the indian anti-dumping cases, the south american and australian agricultural cases and, in general, the extensive and incorrect use of safeguards. in many of the cases brought against the european community, the latter succeeds in obtaining adequate satisfaction for the settlement of disputes in the wto. however, such success is often too late and the damage to european industry is irreparable. in view of the picture presented to us by the executive committee in its report, the committee on international trade could have suggested, in response to a reaction of instinct, that the same methodology and the same behaviour should be adopted by trading partners who are in breach of anti-dumping, anti-subsidy and safeguard rules, but it has not done so. we are convinced that respect for the rules of international trade, established in a multilateral framework, is a basic principle for economic growth and, more generally, for peaceful coexistence between nations. two wrongs never make a right. in this context, we would like to stress that the rules must be applied and that failure to apply them must be met with sanctions that guarantee the right within a short time. if there are no short-term measures, the damage is irreparable. in defence of legality and of the part of european industry which feels unfairly affected by unlawful measures, we call on the commission to pursue decisively the negotiations in the wto, aimed at making the application of trade defence measures by other wto members less arbitrary, by promoting action to make the application of the wto dispute settlement body's decisions faster and more effective. these points should be included in the doha development agenda should these negotiations - as we hope - be resumed. we therefore call on the commission to give due weight to this matter in the context of the initiatives to increase the external competitiveness of european industry which were recently announced by commissioner mandelson before the committee on international trade. finally, we recommend that the commission refrain from granting preferential treatment or favourable treatment to those trading partners who, repeatedly and with serious economic repercussions for european industry, do not act in line with wto rules and jurisprudence. the committee on international trade is of the opinion that in the face of serious situations one cannot remain completely passive. if we are to win the support of the public for the new rules of international trade, we must work for greater transparency, consistency and respect for the law by all actors, by implementing measures ranging from border controls to the application of common sanctions against those who trade in counterfeit or otherwise illegal goods on european territory. we cannot but link the conclusions of this report to the commission's recent initiative for a reform of the european community's anti-dumping and anti-subsidy policy, aimed at limiting the use of these instruments by the commission in the context of a more careful and wider consideration of the community interest.

the commission's vice-president mr president, i would like to thank mrs weiler once again, as well as the rapporteurs for opinions from the various committees: mr langen, mr costa and mrs staniszewska. i will try to answer some of the questions, without claiming to answer all of them. i shall first answer mrs cederschiöld, mr lambsdorff and mrs rühle. when a municipality provides certain services to another public entity for remuneration, these are in principle publicly contracted services. the public entity receiving the contract competes with private companies and possibly other public entities offering the same service. a general exclusion of all forms of public-public cooperation from the scope of the community rules on public procurement and the rules on concessions would therefore be unacceptable. the case law of the court of justice is very clear in this respect. conversely, not all forms of public-public cooperation are covered by community law. the commission acknowledges that clarification is needed to determine the extent to which community law applies to the delegation of tasks to public bodies and which forms of cooperation remain outside the scope of the internal market provisions. we are working closely with all interested parties to bring this clarification. i will then reply to mrs rühle and mrs gebhardt on the issue of public-private partnerships and the concept of 'in house' or 'in control'. the concept of 'in-house' excludes the application of public procurement rules where a public body awards a contract or a concession to a third party over which it exercises a certain degree of control. the court has specified the conditions under which this derogation may be applied. you will understand that the commission wishes to keep this exception to the rules on the award of public contracts within the framework. in particular, it seems extremely difficult that a public contract or a concession could be awarded in a discriminatory manner to an undertaking in which certain private interests are represented, while the other private undertakings concerned are excluded. we therefore believe that it is necessary at this stage to stick to the current definition of the conditions for the application of in-house: the exercise by the local authority of control over the provider which is comparable to that which it exercises over its own services and the performance by the provider of the main part of its activities with the local authority concerned. for these reasons, and also in order not to undermine the new rules on public procurement which are only just being transposed in the member states, it does not seem appropriate to legislate on public-private joint ventures and the concept of in-house. an interpretative communication is the most appropriate way to explain how the rules governing public procurement apply to the selection of private partners for such partnerships. i would like to say to mr savary, who raised the question of double-competition, that we are aware of this problem and, as you have noticed, i have referred to it in my speech. i would like to be very clear: we are not demanding that there be double competition simply because we do not think it is necessary. we explained this in the 2004 green paper on ppps and we intend to make our position clear in the texts we will present in 2007. mr president, i am well aware that i cannot answer all the questions, but i would now like to conclude. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. the commission must first examine more closely the costs and benefits of a binding concession initiative and other measures to address the problems. on the basis of the results of this impact assessment, the commission will decide in a second step, most likely next year, whether the comparison of benefits and costs justifies such a legislative initiative and will prepare, if appropriate, a legislative proposal. the message from all those working in the field of ppp creation is clear: they are calling for practical guidance on how to apply public procurement rules to the creation of such partnerships. the commission intends to provide these guidelines in a non-legislative form for the reasons i have indicated in the introduction. the importance of ppps for the european economy cannot be doubted. i hope that parliament's report will help to clarify the community rules on public procurement of concessions in order to offer the partners conditions of transparent and fair competition. we have understood in this debate that parliament is stressing legal certainty, but you will also have understood the commission's concern to preserve, in an area so essential for investment in europe, the margin of manoeuvre to enable it, while ensuring legal certainty, to invest more broadly where the real needs are. and you have both rightly stressed that these are absolutely essential tools. these are the answers i wanted to give, mr president, and i would like to thank parliament once again for the quality of this debate.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on thursday at 11.30 a.m.

member of the commission. ladies and gentlemen, i will be very brief, because we are now past five minutes past midnight and i think we have to follow very strictly the rules of both the working time directive and the other directives that are in force in europe. so very briefly. the fundamental issue, which has been mentioned twice here, is the view that the commission in its communication has tried to reapply articles 24 and 25 which were rejected by the services directive. i note that this view is not based on truth, since articles 24 and 25 are based on the concept of the country of origin, i.e. that the control is carried out by the country of origin. this is not in the communication, because the communication correctly takes as a starting point the legal situation in question, which says that the control activity takes place in the country of posting of workers, or in the country which has received workers. i would also like to note the agreement in the debate that the directive is capable of working at the moment, but it is very important and necessary to develop and deepen its consistent application, because what is the main problem at the moment is inconsistent application, in particular inconsistent crossborder cooperation between member states. the commission has indicated in its communication the steps it intends to take in this respect, and i think it is our duty to take them as consistently and as quickly as possible. i shall not comment on the individual cases which have been mentioned as typical examples of criticism of the directive or the commission, not because it is not feasible, but because i really respect the working hours of interpreters. so let me just make one last general point. in its communication, the commission first interpreted the judgments of the luxembourg court and interpreted those judgments correctly. furthermore, in the light of its duty as guardian of the treaty, it has expressed its views on certain issues. thirdly, it has proposed and is proposing procedures to improve the implementation of this directive. and so let me close with a final note. a fundamental principle of the legal process of the rule of law and the rule of law is that a law, in this case a directive, can only be used for the purpose for which it is intended. this directive is intended to protect posted workers and not to restrict the free movement of services. thus, from the point of view of that general structure and from the point of view of proportionality, the communication does not restrict the member states from exercising their control activity, does not restrict their ability to exercise it effectively, but the fundamental principle of proportionality applies that the obligations imposed must not be disproportionate in relation to the purpose to which they relate in certain cases, and these cases must always be assessed on a case-by-case basis, as the communication indicates at the end. ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for the attention paid by parliament to this directive, because i share your conviction that it is one of the most important labour market directives in force in the european union, that it is our duty to interpret it correctly and precisely and that it is our duty to implement it as quickly and effectively as possible. let me thank the rapporteur for the work she has done, because the report that has been drawn up is undoubtedly one of the steps along the road i have indicated, namely the effective application of the directive so that it fulfils its purpose. ladies and gentlemen, thank you.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to say at once that in the european union, in comparison with the measure we are considering, there are between 50 and 100 thousand successions by death, and this is a measure which is destined to become the reference point for international law. cross-border successions are a very wide phenomenon, which is facing increasing difficulties and is the source of profound differences between the private international law and substantive law systems of the member states. this often results in obstacles to freedom of movement and the enjoyment of property rights. that is why the committee on legal affairs, which i have the honour of chairing, has decided to take the initiative to simplify succession in europe, using a power conferred on it by article 192, and to ask the commission to adopt a legislative proposal. since we, ladies and gentlemen - and i always think so - unfortunately do not yet have the power of legislative initiative, like all our colleagues in the national parliaments, i am addressing myself to you, commissioner frattini, and asking you, with the force that the qualified majority vote will give - i am sure of this - to commit yourself to our demand, which is decisive in the interests of the citizens of europe. you are well aware that today, in order to acquire the right to inherit property, the rightful owners must initiate proceedings in each country where the property is located. it's not just expensive and time-consuming. the transfer of property by inheritance, being a special form of transfer of society, is linked to affective and personal aspects, to interpersonal relationships which are very complex and which also transcend legal reasons. let me bring you a very personal memory from my youth, when i was in college: professor cariota-ferrara, who wrote his thesis on the right of inheritance, said that the right of inheritance was an affective right, a right that was often suffered. i am convinced, therefore, ladies and gentlemen, and mr president, that our proposal really does make a real contribution to the construction of a people's europe. i thank the committee for the lengthy discussion on this subject, which we have dealt with in all its aspects. i really believe that i am offering parliament a very valid proposal, one which will lead to the advancement of political europe and the europe of the people. i therefore urge you to support this report and ask commissioner frattini to do so on behalf of the european citizens. the report we are proposing sets out the means to ensure that there is one applicable law and one court. the applicable law and the court with jurisdiction must, in general, coincide and the criterion for determining this is also objective: the deceased's habitual residence at the time of death. however, private autonomy is not excluded: the testator may choose which law to apply to the entire succession: the law of his country of residence or the law of the state where he is habitually resident at the time of the choice. the parties concerned, should a dispute arise, will in turn be able to choose the applicable law and the competent court. but the most important thing i would like to say about, and which i believe is the cornerstone of our proposal, is that the report envisages the establishment of a european certificate of succession, which will indicate in a binding manner the law applicable to the succession, the beneficiaries of the estate, the persons responsible for its administration and the powers attaching thereto, and the assets inherited. the certificate will be drawn up in a standard form and will allow the transfer of the property to be recorded in the public registers of the member state where the property is located. in this connection, since mrs berger has carried out a more thorough study than others of this proposal and has tabled five amendments, i should like to say that i am particularly interested in the fact that the certificate has its own compulsiveness, its own consistency, its own certainty. in fact, if this is not established, i believe that the whole structure of the measure will be weakened, that it will lose its effectiveness and become less of a reference point, and that not all the countries of europe, of the community, can take it into account, so that it will end up being a consultative and non-obligatory measure, which will probably weaken, in some way, a force that consists precisely in legal certainty and the ability to reach all citizens, so that they have a concrete possibility of acquiring the inheritance through these instruments. the other amendments, in my view, must be rejected and i would like to make a special appeal to my colleague to reflect and perhaps give the proposal a greater impact, perhaps by withdrawing or by a different solution to the same amendment.
