the seventh framework programme. i would therefore like to express my sincere thanks to mr buzek. the modern world is moving fast. the 20th century was already turbulent and enchanting: it has jumped three eras, from the peasant to the industrial to the post-industrial, and it has gone beyond that in the last two lifetimes. it was then that the eu heads of state or government wrote the prescription for the future with foresight: lisbon 2000 is a ten-year agenda, the time allotted to build europe's research and innovation-based knowledge society. today, however, we must note that progress has been slow, even though the sixth framework programme marked a significant positive change in european policy in this particular strategic area. it's a modest effort compared to the colossal effort of emerging economies: in the last three quarters, investment in r & d in china has risen from usd 12.4 billion to usd 84.6 billion, an increase of 580%. today, china has 12.5 percent of the global market and is the world's second largest producer of high-tech goods. then there is india and the countries of the indo-pacific region, the third scientific and technical pole in the world, which produces 36% of the world's high-tech products, exactly twice as much as all of europe. the conclusion of some analysts, rebus sic stantibus, is catastrophic: in 20 years, 90 percent of the scientists on earth will be living in one of the countries of east asia. in the face of colossal investments in research and development in those countries, some of which exceed 10% of gdp, europe is lagging behind, a prisoner of the selfishness of the member states, some of which still invest less than 1% while the european average remains below 2% of gdp. this, in a very brief way, is the overall picture as we are about to launch the seventh framework programme for which the european commission rightly asked the member states for a more significant financial effort. the people programme is the body and mind of the whole legislative body: healthy mind in a healthy body. hence the idea of motivating researchers to motivate research. the seventh framework programme is the birth of the european researcher, free, independent and motivated. this is the context we are dealing with: from recognition of the profession of researcher to legal status; from a code of conduct to the creation of a database for the selection and recruitment of researchers; the alignment of remuneration with the best international standards, equal opportunities for men and women, with measures to protect women researchers, and the reconciliation of their family and professional lives; the commission will continue to support the development of the european social model, in particular through the creation of a european social area, the development of a european social area and the development of a european social area. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. to abandon them would be a gift to the united states or china. the positive experience of the marie curie actions is appropriately reviewed and will be continued, giving substance and breath to the project aiming at excellence as added value, with a structuring effect on the european research area. it also provides for partnerships and equal opportunities between the public and private sectors. last but not least, intellectual property, on which the council has behaved a bit like pilate with jesus of nazareth: he took the idea and turned it into a standard of address. no, this is not good! if we really want to motivate the researcher, we must give him a concrete guarantee of the protection of the rights arising from the intellectual property he has produced. this is possible - i insist on asking the commission and the council to do so - by means of private law contractual clauses, which protect the results of the research and the individual researcher. to excel, we must motivate and attract researchers from all over the world by offering attractive conditions. in order to combine quantity and quality and to produce excellence in basic and technological research, as the people programme and the seventh framework programme aim to do, all the links must be made and all the open problems must be solved, industry and private investment must be safeguarded and stimulated, without, however, at the same time, mortifying the engine, the heart and the mind of research which is and remains man. i thank you the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank commissioner potočnik and the finnish presidency for the work they have carried out over the last few years. before i talk about the specific programme for which i am the rapporteur, namely the euratom specific programme, i should like to make a few comments on the seventh framework programme and the specific programmes. i congratulate mr buzek and all the other rapporteurs on the excellent teamwork which led us to launch the seventh framework programme at the last possible moment. the bitterness remains, however, that we have not made a qualitative leap, that is to say, the doubling of the number of seats on which many hopes were based and which would have been a strong signal, a signal of europe's importance and above all of its conviction that it would achieve the lisbon objective. the doubling has not happened, but we are still trying to get a result. i shall start with the last comment made by commissioner potočnik on cooperation, concerning a concern i have expressed on behalf of myself and my group about the risk of funding bodies or entities under the seventh framework programme that have been established or are operating in breach of international law. the issue has been discussed recently by the european parliament, with particular reference to the entity established in the occupied territories west bank, gaza and east jerusalem although it has a more general value. i would like to stress that this concern also applies to situations, for example, in scientific associations, which may be eligible for calls for proposals under the seventh framework programme, even if they are based on national laws which violate international laws, for example by preventing the free participation of individuals and ethnic and religious groups in research activities. i believe that this is the problem on which the commission is called upon to express its views. i was not satisfied with the answer given on this point, because it seems to me to be limited to a very specific area, whereas i believe it should be addressed to a more general area. as regards the specific programmes, i am generally satisfied with most of the results achieved and i would particularly like to emphasize the attention paid to researchers. i believe that many of the activities of modern, complex society are increasingly based on the human factor. it is obviously impossible to think about european research without thinking about researchers and their needs for mobility, training and status, which are expressed in the charter of the rights of researchers. the seventh framework programme will have to put in place measures to ensure the best working conditions for european scientists, including to stem and possibly counteract the trend of brain drain to other parts of the world. i very much appreciated the effort to focus on basic research by creating an entity independent of the commission, which would be responsible for providing a merit judgment on the excellence of the scientific proposal to be funded under the seventh framework programme. the effectiveness of this new body will be measured by its ability to be authoritative in the selection of proposals and to earn the respect of the scientific community. only then will it be able to attract innovative proposals and finance ambitious projects that raise the quality of european research. transparency of operation, including through parliament's involvement in the evaluation of the work of this body, will be essential to its success. i should now like to take the remaining minutes to speak about the euratom specific programme. i agree with the commission's position, as expressed by mr buzek on the euratom framework programme, and i believe that europe must focus on the development of fusion, so that in the long term it can become an essential, unlimited, environmentally acceptable and economically competitive source of energy, capable of making an important contribution to a sustainable and secure energy supply. iter is a key step on the road to the use of fusion energy. after lengthy negotiations on the site of the reactor, the project partners have finally signed the international iter agreement. the successful conclusion of the negotiations, namely the choice to build iter at the european site of caradache in france, requires the adoption of determined and coherent measures by the union, within the framework of this and subsequent framework programmes. there is therefore a need to set up a european iter agency, in the form of a joint venture under the euratom treaty, to provide the means to fulfil europe's international obligations under the iter agreement, which means the construction of the machine and collaborative projects with japan. this agency, based in barcelona, should have as its first objective the realisation of iter. i think, however, that the use of the agency should be limited to this and i do not share the commission's position that the whole field of fusion research should be entrusted to one agency. i do not mean to undermine the agency's role, which i believe is important, but i think it is essential to help it achieve the objective which is already quite complicated. i also believe that european research needs to be more independent, and this is also true in some ways of the european research centre. on the other hand, the associations of the european fusion development agreement (efda) have over the years proved to play an essential role. europe is leading this programme because it has demonstrated the quality of its research in the field. building iter is only the first step, as we need to use it and make the best use of it, through a new generation of researchers and high-value research in europe. this can be ensured by keeping construction and research separate, which will continue to be carried out with existing machines as iter is built. that is why i think it is important, as was the case with the buzek report, that my amendment be adopted in the house.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank parliament and in particular the rapporteur, mrs lynn, for putting this important question on the agenda for today's plenary session. i am glad that parliament and the commission are very close in their views on the disabled. in particular, i would like to thank parliament for its support in the development and implementation of the european disability strategy. it is not just about giving people with disabilities the opportunity to enjoy their rights, their rights to human dignity, to equal treatment, to independence from other people and to full inclusion in society. disabled people must be able to exercise their abilities and participate in social and economic life. the commission's action plan on equal opportunities for people with disabilities provides a strategic framework for setting current priorities. as mrs lynn's report emphasises, the community's policies and activities have a wide range of effects on the situation of people with disabilities. in 2003, the council therefore also recommended that member states should fully follow the action plan in designing their policies for people with disabilities. at the end of 2005, i presented a communication on equal opportunities for disabled people, which launched the second phase of the european union's action plan for disabled people 2006-07. this second stage is also the subject of mrs lynn's report. first, the current situation. the statistics available to the commission speak for themselves. 44.6 million people of working age, that's one in six of our fellow citizens, have a long-term health problem or disability, by their own estimate. the employment rate of disabled people is up to 40%, compared with 64.2% for non-disabled people. even for those with relatively mild disabilities, the employment rate does not exceed 50%. 43.7% of disabled people who are not working believe that they could work if they had access to adequate assistance. the commission's 2006/07 programme aims to respond to this situation. in particular, an environment must be created that enables persons with disabilities to enjoy their rights, to have the same choice as non-disabled persons, to make decisions about their lives, to participate in the economic activities of life, to exercise their abilities in both their personal and professional lives and to fulfil their obligations as any other citizen. in this spirit, four priority areas have been identified for the period 2006-07. the european council also identified the promotion of employment and labour participation of people with disabilities as a priority at its spring 2006 meeting. access to quality, accessible and affordable services for people with disabilities must be a key element of the european action programme for the coming years. access by persons with disabilities to material goods and services is essential to ensure the exercise of their civil rights and independence. the union needs to be better able to analyse the situation and identify the development factors that affect the status of persons with disabilities. this action plan has already produced positive results. the first european legislation specifically relating to disabled people was adopted, namely the regulation on the rights and obligations of disabled people in the field of air transport, which was cited by the rapporteur. the rules applicable to the new structural funds guarantee the right of access of persons with disabilities to projects financed by the community and provide that the principle of accessibility must be respected at all stages of the fund's operation. the recent adoption of the united nations convention on the rights of persons with disabilities is a landmark event. for the first time in history, the european community is a party to the convention. the convention firmly enshrines the fundamental principles of the european union's disability strategy, namely non-discrimination, equal opportunities and active action for social inclusion.
the european action plan 2006-2007 for persons with disabilities sets out a strategy based on the principle of non-discrimination in the access to goods and services for every european citizen. this is a culture no longer linked to the idea of passive care but to the objective of integration, active participation in economic and social life and the recognition of the protection of their rights. the quality of life is a central theme, so that people with disabilities can fulfil their expectations while respecting human dignity. this is why the relationship between health and the environment in which we live is also emphasized. we share the articulation of the three objectives: complete the implementation of the equal treatment in employment and working conditions directive; to strengthen the integration of disability issues into relevant community policies; to improve accessibility for all. our amendments have highlighted the need for a generally homogeneous approach in all the member states in the field of transport and mobility, and to ensure adequate assistance in the school and training process and in the family, as well as the promotion of sign language. it is also essential to stress the need to establish and guarantee high european quality standards in the provision of social services, because it is the quality perceived by the person that determines the quality of a full life in the future. we hope that the statement of principle will be followed by more and more practical action. finally, i would like to thank mrs lynne for her work.
i am most convinced that the lynne report is right, because it has been able to grasp the problems of the complex world of disability in a broad way, and to propose actions and instruments which are sufficiently appropriate to meet the needs of life, relationships and social position. i would also like to express the hope that the statements of principle, which are acceptable, will be followed by more and more concrete action by the executive committee, and that the 'differently-abled' (or, if you prefer, the 'differently-abled') will be able to achieve their life expectancies in a way that respects their human dignity. the text we are about to vote on summarises well the work done by the rapporteur in our committee and the social demands coming from the various national realities. i would stress in this connection the need for the behaviour of the member states of the european community to be more or less homogeneous, in order to avoid unjustified equalisation between european citizens on the grounds of geographical differences.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in the days since the agreement with the council was reached - which was also made possible thanks to the support of the commission - i have been wondering what we could have compared with this long march, which, as far as i am concerned, has lasted three and a half years and has brought us to this point. to answer that question, i had to draw on my passion for mountaineering: perhaps the most apt analogy is to say that we have climbed a great mountain, probably, and without exaggeration, an 8,000-meter himalayan. i've never been this high, and i don't think i'll ever get there because i'm a modest climber, but i know what happens when you get to the top: at that point, the effort, the risk, and perhaps the dissatisfaction that often comes with reaching the top and the view is modest because of the fog, don't matter. it 's happened to me many times: i come, and i don't see anything! but the satisfaction is still great. the important thing is to be clear about two things: the first is to know if you've really reached the top, and the second is to prepare well for the descent, which is often no easier than the climb. as the coordinator, i would like to give my opinion on these two aspects. did we really get to the top? i think so. with the package of chapters we have settled in the final stage of the negotiations on duty of care, animal welfare and, above all, the promotion of alternative methods to animal testing, the agency, the communication of information, the adaptation to the new interinstitutional agreement on comitology - thus safeguarding the role of parliament. we have had to make a compromise, however, in the form of the extension of the chemical safety report to small tonnages, which was not a victim of this ascent, but an early return to the baseline, since we have defined a revision rule which will allow us to possibly reintroduce this obligation in seven years' time, once the appropriate checks have been carried out along the entire supply chain. in this agreement we have above all succeeded in resolving well - and that is why we have come to the top - the most controversial issue, the purpose of reach, namely the regulation of the substances of greatest concern through the authorization procedure. to assess whether we've really reached the top, we need to remember where we started: from a valley far, far away. the original commission proposal provided that all substances subject to authorization could be authorized on the basis of the principle of adequate control. she's come a long way. the council's common position, which was positively influenced by parliament, has already reduced the area of these substances and, subsequently, with the agreement reached on 30 november, we have taken a further step forward by reducing the number of substances that can be adapted by this shorter and simpler route and then we have included all substances - including those which will be authorized on the basis of adequate control - in a substitution process. where an alternative exists, a replacement plan must be submitted; where no alternatives exist at the time of authorization, the research and development lines which the undertaking intends to pursue must in any case be stated. on this basis, therefore, the duration of the authorisation will be decided on a case-by-case basis and will have to be justified by the commission if an alternative exists. and if an alternative emerges during the authorisation process, the obligation to replace the plan will be triggered. what i would like to stress is that the commission will take its decisions on a case-by-case basis on the basis of the opinion of the agency, which will have to take account of the opinions of the economic and social committee and the risk assessment committee, which will also have to take account of the contributions of third parties. it is therefore a very transparent process and not just a matter of self-declaration by the applicant. as far as the descent from the summit is concerned, i think it is important to choose the best route, since the same degree of difficulty can be increased considerably compared to the ascent. and by that metaphor i mean that we have to adopt the compromise we have reached, because that will allow the regulation to be published by the end of the year and thus the deadline for the entry into force of reach by 1 june 2007 can be met. this is a complex issue, which cannot be resolved in a hurry: reach is so complicated that it is wrong to expect to solve all the problems at the approval stage. the important thing now is to launch the application: we have foreseen several mechanisms and deadlines, so to speak self-regulating ones, which will allow for adjustments in the course of the work, on the basis of the practical experience we have gained. we have improved the balance through all the steps of this procedure, i am thinking of the answers we have given to the problems of small businesses, i am thinking of strengthening the protection of health and the environment, with particular regard to the risks to workers. i think that, on the whole, this finished product can be evaluated very positively. i have noticed that my friends in the green group and the gue group have tabled a package of amendments, which are all very welcome, and which are very similar to those which i proposed in the negotiations with the council and the commission to get us to where we are now. what are these amendments for? to get where? what peak could be reached in an unlikely compromise? we all know what the real alternative is: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. let's face it, it might be better. that is the real alternative we have and i am sure that parliament will make the right choice in the vote on wednesday. mr president, with my speech today, i have finished my work: the vote list will also be small, there is no big job, it is only two pages, a record for reach, considering that some 5000 amendments were evaluated at first reading. my work is therefore over here, and i would just like to thank all those who have taken part in various ways in this himalayan expedition. many have participated: i have met six presidencies, many committee leaders and commissioners, and i was always there, playing the lead, even though sometimes someone, instead of giving me security, tried i believe that behind the revision of the previous legislation - seen as a natural legal adaptation to new technologies - there is a desire to liberalize the advertising market wildly: no daily limit on telesales, telepromotions not included in the time limit, unregulated minispot and the introduction of product placement, an advertising practice which is so interwoven with the content of the programmes that it cannot be regulated either quantitatively or qualitatively. the text of the directive also lacks binding references to the principles of pluralism, independence and free competition which should form the basis of any broadcasting system in a modern democracy, as parliament itself has repeatedly stated. television is undoubtedly the most important cultural medium of our time, linked by a double thread to the democratic and cultural life of a country, and it is dangerous to make its contents and its operation dependent on the logic of the market alone, without protecting the rights of viewers, for example, to unbiased information or to the protection of children. how can you protect your children from food-altering commercials? it's a fact that most kids today only eat foods that are high in sugar and fat. in this commission proposal, which is 'borderless', that is to say, without limits, there is only advertising. without the course correction proposed by the amendments tabled by the gue, but also by a cross-cutting group of members of parliament with no political ties, the television of the future risks being enslaved by advertising laws alone.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the aim of this directive is to liberalize the advertising market completely, and this leads to a single model of television, a television exclusively for entertainment. it will become impossible to make quality, educational, cultural television. the european cultural production will be seriously damaged and this directive will cause serious damage to newspapers, which will no longer have the possibility of intercepting advertising. television often induces superfluous needs and advertising thus becomes an assembly line of induced needs: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. this evil deed of product placement is changing the very nature of advertising, which is transformed from the soul of commerce into the very soul of television broadcasting. a leading liberal philosopher like karl popper called television a "bad teacher". today, with this directive, the proclamations of the "bad teacher" become "borderless".

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i speak on behalf of the new psi. i attended an interesting international conference in brussels last week on the role of the eu in promoting democracy in the world. many representatives of third countries expressed their confidence in the eu's support for democratization processes and thus for the promotion of geopolitical stability and world peace. the enlargement process and the neighbourhood policy have both proved to be valuable tools for achieving these objectives. i have come to realise that expectations are very high, but also that the democratic process in europe is still sometimes imperfect and that some institutional adjustments are needed. the plan d proposed for the current year by the committee on democracy, dialogue and debate is a first step in the right direction, but for the eu to play its rightful role at international and foreign policy level, it is important that it first tackles some basic issues that can no longer be postponed. for the sake of brevity, i shall mention three: the first is the ratification of the constitution, the second is the question of the single seat at the un and, last but not least, energy autonomy. the eu must be able to relaunch a strategic plan for renewable and alternative energy so that it no longer has a weak position vis-à-vis its major partners and can act decisively, that is, regardless of economic interests, even in the most serious crises.

vice-chairman of the commission . mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am particularly grateful to the few members present in this chamber, perhaps fewer than ten, for discussing a subject which affects many tens of millions of young people and very young people, our children, in the european union. the protection of the rights and fundamental rights of young people must continue to be a high priority for the european union. it is a priority for the european commission, and i must say frankly that the acts of violence and sadism that emerge through some particularly bloody video games are a cause of great concern to us. new technologies, the ability of young people and very young people to operate on the internet, on technological games, have changed the relationship between adults and children. often, kids, our kids, know technology much better than adults. the first thing that is needed is a stronger sense of responsibility and awareness on the part of adults and parents, and attention and education so that parents can make informed choices, with full awareness of the risks. there's a system of classifying, labeling content in movies, but also in games and video games, which can help. of course, it must be combined with a mechanism of stronger education. these are necessary components if we are to achieve an effective solution. the european union already has the means to combat these worrying phenomena in the context of policies concerning justice, security prevention, but also the information society and the rules on the internal market. i must say frankly, ladies and gentlemen, that i have also greatly appreciated certain initiatives to monitor and strengthen the protection of minors which were announced to me by certain ministers of the interior before and after the council of ministers and which have been taken up by certain national political forces in certain member states. i am referring in particular to the increase in controls on the sale of particularly violent games and video games to minors. it's equally important, i think, to hold game producers accountable. in 2003, a european self-regulatory system, called pan european game information, was adopted to help parents make choices when buying video games for minors. this system of self-regulation is supported by a large majority of producers. it was developed after consultation with industry, parents' associations and consumer associations. it covers 27 countries and contains the indication of a minimum age for access to a given game and the obligation to describe the content of a game or video game that is marketed. this system, ladies and gentlemen, helps parents to choose - provided that it is the parents who decide which video game their children buy - but it does not concern and does not contain any reference to the content of the video game. this self-regulation was established, on the one hand, to protect minors, but, on the other, also to respect another fundamental principle, such as freedom of expression. i intend to meet very soon with the producers and their representative associations in order to assess the relevance, i would say the timeliness, of the indicators contained in the self-regulation programme. i think it is time to assess whether those indicators have not worked as we would have liked. as regards the content of games or video games that can be found on the internet, there are systems in the world, but they are applied and implemented on the initiative of certain authoritative consortia: the first is what we call the platform for internet content selection and the second is what we call the recreational software advisory council, both of which are located primarily in the united states. i should like to point out, however, that neither the un report on violence against young people nor the world health organisation's report on violence and health analyses this phenomenon, which is merely mentioned as if it were not absolutely necessary to go into it. in 2005, we as the european commission carried out a study funded by the daphne programme. this survey, based on a number of studies relating to the violent video game industry, highlights the need for a multidisciplinary approach, which is currently lacking. one of the findings of this study is that the influence of violent images on young people cannot be denied. however, it can manifest itself in different ways depending on various factors. for example, the welfare, the situation of the young person, where he lives, whether there is an active presence of the parents who are with him or not, the control over access to the media and the internet by young people, the fact that parents exercise or not control over whether children can access the internet in absolute freedom, the level of education that is given, the socioeconomic level of the family. all these factors have an impact on how the violent effect can be reflected in the minds and minds of the young and the very young. there are other important factors to consider: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. when i speak of monitoring the sale of violent video games, i mean actual monitoring, because today there are no mandatory instruments to check whether a young person under 16 can buy video games that incite or glorify acts of violence and perhaps actual criminal acts. i think this house will at least want to consider this problem, also taking into account the fact that the programmes which daphne has funded against violence against young people are based on this very point: how to protect the young and the very young. in conclusion, following the strategy we launched in july for the protection of children, i intend to put this problem to the european forum for the rights of the child. as you know, this forum was set up in early 2007. at the first useful meeting of the forum, i intend to open a public and transparent discussion with all the stakeholders concerned, the non-governmental organisations, the member states, the parents' associations, the children, the minors and also with the national ombudsmen responsible for youth rights. the four key words on this topic are: parents, media and education professionals, producers - because if you do not prevent the production of these violent games you do not address the problem at its root - and, finally, politics. it is about examining how policy can develop a strategy that, without acts of censorship, substantially protects children. these are the pillars with which we must approach the question i have put to you tonight. in the spring, i'll be submitting a paper on cybercrime. i believe that the crimes, the offenses against the law, the violations committed through the internet make young people and the very young particularly vulnerable victims. it is our political, institutional and moral duty to react seriously, with a european strategy, against the incitement to violence, against the glorification of violence, against the glorification of violence.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank commissioner frattini in particular for the very concrete proposals he has put forward to us this evening. there is no doubt that europe is witnessing a worrying exponential growth in incidents of violence, bullying and violence between children, and it is undeniable that television and the internet are shaping the behaviour of our children, as is the spread of violent video games, which are increasing in number and with increasingly brutal content. i'll give you an example. there's the very recent video game rule of rose, which is something really serious because it's a video game that has children as its protagonists and many of the images are borderline sexual perversion and sadism. we therefore welcome the debate which is taking place, even though - as the president pointed out - it was confined to a night time with very few participants. it's a shame, really. however, we want some action to be taken on this subject, certainly not by censorship, as commissioner reding has already said, but we share his initiative, commissioner frattini, to send a letter to the eu interior ministers asking for a careful review of the controls on violence in video games. after the words of commissioner reding, we expect the pegi (pan-european game information) system to become a more effective monitoring body. in conclusion, we strongly urge that concrete instruments be identified to control and prohibit the distribution of violent video games and that a kind of european observatory on children and minors be set up, also to monitor the contents of games and video games in advance and, if possible, to draw up a single code for the marketing and distribution of video games for minors.

the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the committee on transport unanimously adopted an opinion on the langen report, in which it stressed the need to make choices which stabilise investment in the medium to long term and which give certainty to investors, producers and consumers. i'd like this to be shot in full force. in addition, there is a need for greater clarity in the definition of second generation biofuels, in relation to the environmental impacts that their use and production may cause. it is not the same to talk about biomass from waste rather than from forestry waste or something else. it is also necessary to clarify the number of previous directives which have accompanied the policy of support for biofuels, since there are some inconsistencies which must be overcome, and above all the existing directive on the quality of fuels for blending with petrol must be redefined.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i speak on behalf of the new psi. i not only welcome the commission's green paper and mrs morgan's report on a sustainable european energy policy, but i hope that this strategy will become one of the priorities of our union as from 2007. as i had the opportunity to reiterate yesterday in this chamber and on other occasions, the eu's ability to implement an energy strategy - not only sustainable but also autonomous - and therefore its independence from the power games and economic interests that often play a role in this sector, are the key factors in many of the global challenges that lie ahead in the near future, not only in terms of competitiveness but also in terms of the political and strategic weight that the union wants and can achieve. rather than finalising strategic agreements with existing and potential partners, research efforts should be stepped up and member states should be allowed to make the most of their sustainable energy resources, each according to its own characteristics and potential.

on behalf of the green group in the european parliament. mr president, i would like to thank the finnish presidency for the generous commitment with which it has tackled issues of great importance immigration, the constitution, climate change although we would hope that you too, with a healthy nordic realism, would come with us to the conclusion that nuclear energy has nothing to do with solving the problem of climate change or emissions, as the delays of your new plant, its prohibitive costs and the great difficulties of its construction clearly demonstrate, and as the series of accidents that have occurred in recent months in different european locations, but which have been completely silenced, also demonstrate. in conclusion, i should like to thank the presidency and say that i am very much perplexed by the way the debate has developed, which calls this summit a council for a europe of results. what are we talking about? the previous finnish presidency in tampere had achieved much more on the immigration issue. on the question of enlargement, ten years ago, before the accession of finland, sweden and austria, we in this parliament fought a very great battle to ensure that the issues of the constitution and institutional renewal were tackled earlier and better than a rapid enlargement which was certainly not good for the majority of our citizens. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i hope that the council will be able to accept them. the text that was rejected in the referenda will obviously not be the same as the one that will be drawn up and that we will obviously have to seek alliances, inside and outside the european institutions, in order to solve the great problem of institutional reforms. we were also convinced, together with a group of members of this parliament, that before cyprus could be admitted to our union, the problem of the division of the island had to be solved, and today we inherit this lack of resolve from the european union as a whole. so, frankly, i see nothing particularly new or concrete. am i happy about this? no, i am not happy, but i do see the need for transparency, including with regard to our citizens. it is obvious that we are in full agreement with the idea that turkey should remain a partner, that there should be further enlargements and that the balkans should be given an unambiguous prospect of accession. at the same time, however, we cannot accept the hypocrisy which is being presented as a great novelty, namely that to speak today of institutional reform is to some extent to impede enlargement. we cannot accept it, because it is not and it does not have to be. before i thank mr poettering, mr president, i would like to make one final point on the subject of relations with russia. we must be absolutely aware that the best policy to adopt in relation to prime minister putin is a policy which makes us self-sufficient, or at least as self-sufficient as possible, which means reducing our consumption by 30% and promoting renewable energies even more convincingly. otherwise, we'll always be dependent, if not on russia, then on someone else. i too, mr president, would like to thank mr poettering for his kindness to us and also for the fact that in some cases we have been able to work together quite well. on behalf of my group, i wish him all the best for his future - which depends partly on mine, but we shall see - and i hope that he will always be able to fight for europe, because this parliament really needs it, following the line of conduct established in a certain way by president borrell, who tried to carry forward - with greater or lesser difficulty than his troops - the idea of an autonomous parliament. i hope that you too - and i would like to make this personal note - will in future, if parliament gives you a majority, be willing to leave aside certain accents that are a little too close to a religion, which are not good for europe or for parliament.
